Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is the use of antiretroviral medication to prevent acquisition of HIV infection in appropriate persons; it should be used in combination with other HIV prevention methods. What is Pre Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Men who have sex with men (MSM) Heterosexual women and men with concurrent or high number of sex partners (greater than 1 new sex partner within the last 3 months or greater than 1 sexual partner) Transgender women Women and men whose partners are known to have HIV infection Young women and men at substantial risk of HIV infection Female and male sex workers Individuals with recurrent STIs Persons with repeated use of Post Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) (PEP use greater than twice within a 6-month period) Target Populations 1

The PrEP continuum begins with the identification of individuals at high-risk for HIV acquisition (from the target populations) and takes them through the process of interest, screening for eligibility, PrEP initiation, adherence and retention. The continuum also makes provisions for persons who may decide to discontinue (cycle off) PrEP. PrEP Continuum of Care It takes at least 7 days before PrEP becomes effective in both men and women. If they wish to discontinue PrEP, it must be continued for at least 7 days after the most recent exposure before it is stopped. PrEP should be taken every day at the same time. If a dose is missed on a given day but realized on the same day, then it should be taken when remembered. If a dose is missed but not remembered, there is no need to take two pills the next day. They should continue with one tablet once daily. Condom use is still advised, as PrEP does not protect against other STIs. Clients should be advised that: 2

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of Tenofovir/Emtricitabine one (1) table for 7 days after last exposure to prevent the acquisition of HIV. If a person using oral PrEP tests positive for HIV, oral PrEP should be stopped immediately and the person referred for prompt initiation of HIV treatment on Tenofovir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir (TLD) and linked to a treatment site for continued follow up care. Transition from oral PrEP to HIV treatment without gaps avoids the possibility of resurgence in viral load, immunological injury, and secondary transmissions. Tracking seroconversion is important in informing gaps in care and in identifying needs for increased outreach to oral PrEP clients if continuation is an issue. Hepatitis B vaccination is appropriate for people at substantial risk of HBV or HIV infection. Vaccination is warranted if there is no documented history of a completed vaccine series for HBV. PrEP can be provided whether or not HBV vaccination is available. Tenofovir (TDF) is active against HBV infection at the same dose used for PrEP. WHO recommends TDF for treatment of HBV infection in people for whom treatment is indicated. Not all people with chronic HBV infection have treatment indications. If PrEP is stopped prior to three months in a patient who has HBV they can experience a HBV infection flare, thus it is recommended that a complete three months of Tenofovir (TDF) be administered as well as referral and follow up with a gastroenterologist. Indications for treatment of HBV should be assessed according to national guidelines Management of Hepatitis B (HBV) Infection 9

Event-driven PrEP (ED-PrEP) is the use of a short dosing course of antiretroviral medication that is taken before and after sex to prevent the acquisition of HIV infection. Event Driven PrEP Eligibility for Event Driven (ED) PrEP Persons eligible for ED PrEP Persons not eligible for ED PrEP Men who have sex with men: Who would find ED-PrEP more effective and convenient Who have infrequent sex (for example, sex less than 2 times per week on average) Who are able to plan for sex at least 2 hours in advance, or who can delay sex for at least 2 hours Women or transgender women Transgender men having vaginal sex Men having vaginal or anal sex with women People with chronic hepatitis B infection 10

Algorithm for offering ED PrEP 11 Assess HIV risk and determine eligibility for oral PrEP in men who have sex with men Follow-up visit (1 month after initiation and/or every 3 months) Provide testing for HIV and other STIs Oﬀer counselling by discussing adherence to dosing strategy during use, and if PrEP user transitions from one dosing strategy to another Assess if HIV risk is likely to persist in the next few weeks and months Adolescent men who have sex with men may require more active support in continuing on PrEP, whichever dosing strategy is chosen Men who have sex with men on PrEP can switch from daily dosing to ED-PrEP (and vice-versa) Daily dosing if risk is more frequent than 2 times per week and sex cannot be predicted or delayed by 2 hours. Event-driven dosing if sex can be predicted (particularly for infrequent sex) Oﬀer PrEP and discuss dosing options Figure 3. Algorithm for assessment of clients for ED PrEP

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 12 FOREWARD Tuberculosis (TB) is endemic to the Jamaican population. National statistics over the past 15 years have not indicated a resurgence in the disease occurrence. However, the concern exists that the HIV/AIDS epidemic will increase the risk factors of infection, and the number of co-infected cases will invariably increase the prevalence of the disease. The main objective of this manual is to provide and promote standardized procedures for the prevention and control of TB in Jamaica. Successful implementation of the policy package is dependent largely on the commitment of health professionals at all levels in the health sector. It will serve as a management tool, equipping health professionals with the necessary technical resource to effectively manage any eventualities they may encounter in case management. Establishment of the new manual will also satisfy the requisition by the World Health Organization (WHO) global TB strategy, for member countries to provide a procedure manual that will serve as a management tool and as a training resource manual. The manual will emphasize the modern strategy for treatment as recommended by the WHO and will incorporate the short course chemotherapeutic regime as applied under the directly observed treatment, short course (DOTS) management strategy. This is in keeping with the key strategy of any National Tuberculosis Programme (NTP); which is the early detection and cure of all infectious cases. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 14 I. POLICIES, STRUCTURES, GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 1.1 Policies 1.2 Structures 1.3 Epidemiology 1.4 Targets 1.5 Objectives 1.6 Key Strategies

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 15 1.1 Policies Jamaica is a party to several TB related resolutions endorsed at the different sittings of the PAHO Directing Council and the World Health Assembly. The management of the National Tuberculosis Programme lies within the HIV/STI/TB Unit of the Ministry of Health and Wellness, and receives oversight from the Health Promotion and Protection Branch. The TB policy and procedure manual is developed to provide a standardized approach to the management of TB in Jamaica. It is in line with the National Strategic Plan for Tuberculosis 2020 – 2024 goal, targets and objectives; and the guiding principles of the World Health Organization END TB Strategy, adapted for the Jamaican context. TB is classified as a Class 1 Notifiable Disease, governed under the Public Health (Class 1 Notifiable Diseases) Order, 2003. Accordingly, the case must be reported within twenty- four hours of being discovered to the parish Public Health Department or the National Surveillance Unit of the Ministry of Health and Wellness. The National Chest Hospital (NCH), the Bustamante Hospital for Children (BHC) and the Cornwall Regional Hospital (CRH) serve as the primary diagnostic and management centers for TB cases in Jamaica.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 16 1.2 Structures The National Tuberculosis Prevention and Control Programme (NTPCP) is managed at three levels: 1. Central level – policies, guidelines, regulations, monitoring and evaluation 2. Regional level – supervision of operations 3. Parish level – implementation of policies and guidelines Central Level The management of the National Tuberculosis Programme at the central level involves the National Public Health Laboratory, the HIV/STI/TB and National Surveillance Units of the Ministry of Health and Wellness; and the National Health Fund. The central level develops, implements, monitors, and evaluates all aspects of the TB programme including development of guidelines, monitoring and evaluation and the procurement of drugs and laboratory supplies. Drugs are procured and distributed by the National Health Fund (NHF) and diagnostic services provided by the National Public Health Laboratory. Regional Level The Regional Health Authorities (RHAs) are charged with the supervision of the Parish operations within the RHAs and serve as the connection between the National and Parish levels. Parish Level The Parish level is responsible for the implementation of the policies and guidelines and ensuring the activities of the National Tuberculosis Programme are delivered at the end user level. This involves case detection, referral for and completion of treatment and investigation of contacts.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 17 1.3 Epidemiology Jamaica is currently classified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a low-burden (less than 10 cases per 100,000 population per year) TB country with an estimated incidence of 2.9 per 100,000 population (n=80) in 2018 (Source: NSU). During the five- year period 2014 -2018, there were 544 cases of Tuberculosis diagnosed (confirmed) and treated in Jamaica, an average of 109 cases per annum. Of the confirmed cases of Tuberculosis for the period, most (58%) resided in the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA) and 28.6% resided in the area administered by the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA). Together, the SERHA and WRHA consistently contributed over 80% of the confirmed tuberculosis cases identified in the 5-year period. In 2018, there were 80 cases of confirmed TB in Jamaica, of these 59 were male and 21 female (2.8:1), consistent with the global TB picture of a greater incidence in males than females (2:1). The largest number of cases was detected in adults between 25 and 34 years old (n=16; 20%), and this was consistent across the 5-year span between 2014 and 2018. Of the cases confirmed in 2018, 3.8% (n=3) were hypertensive, 2.5% (n=2) diabetic and 1.25% (n=1) had sickle cell disease and asthma respectively. The WHO defines a TB death as a patient who died on treatment for any reason before or during the course of treatment. Adequate disease control measures are expected to result in a case fatality rate of 5% or less. In 2018, 4 (5.0%) persons diagnosed with TB died while on treatment.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 18 1.4 Goal The Goal of the Tuberculosis Programme is to reduce the incidence and mortality from Tuberculosis, thereby accelerating the elimination of Tuberculosis in Jamaica; no family should face catastrophic costs due to Tuberculosis. The achievement of this goal is through the adaptation of the action framework and guiding principles from the World Health Organization (WHO) END TB Strategy for low incidence countries. The priority action areas include: 1) Ensure political commitment, funding and stewardship for planning and essential services of high quality 2) Address the most vulnerable and hard to reach groups 3) Address special needs of migrants and cross-border issues 4) Undertake screening for active TB and Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) in TB contacts and selected high-risk groups and provide appropriate treatment 5) Optimize the prevention and care of drug-resistant TB 6) Ensure continued surveillance, programme monitoring and evaluation and case- based data management 7) Invest in research and new tools 8) Support global TB prevention, care and control

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 19 1.5 Targets of the National Tuberculosis Programme include: Targets to be achieved by 2025: 1. 75% reduction in Tuberculosis deaths (compared with 2015) 2. 50% reduction in Tuberculosis incidence rate (compared to 2015) 3. No affected families facing catastrophic costs due to Tuberculosis 4. To maintain case detection rates of ≥ 85 percent of expected cases 5. To achieve a cure rate of ≥ 90 percent of confirmed cases Targets to be achieved by 2035: 1. 95% reduction in TB deaths (compared to 2015) 2. 90% reduction in TB incidence rate (compared to 2015) 3. No affected families facing catastrophic costs due to TB.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 20 1.6 Key Strategies The key strategies of the Tuberculosis Programme are aimed to: 1. Reduce morbidity and mortality associated with the disease by decreasing or interrupting tuberculosis transmission in Jamaica. 2. Cure the disease in affected individuals, to preserve or quickly restore their work capacity allowing them to remain with their family and community and in this way, maintain their socio-economic position. 3. Decrease the risk of tuberculosis infection in the community and by this means, improve the control situation of tuberculosis, and thus the health, social and economic condition of the community. To achieve this there are three Strategic Interventions with specific strategic actions as outlined below. 1. Integrated Patient-Centered Care and Prevention of TB Strategic Actions: 1.1 Revamp the NTP and strengthen its capacity for management and technical programming. 1.2 Rapidly increase early and appropriate diagnosis of TB. 1.3 Implement vigorous advocacy, communication and social mobilization (ACSM). 1.4 Implement active case finding activities in vulnerable populations. 1.5 Ensure timely and appropriate management of drug-susceptible and drug- resistant TB. 1.6 Strengthen the integration of TB and HIV care to optimize the management of co-infected patients. 1.7 Promote joint management of other co-morbidities associated with TB. 1.8 Review and strengthen the management of latent TB infection. 2. Promote Universal Access to Care for TB Strategic Actions: 2.1 Increase allocation of human and financial resources to the TB control programme. 2.2 Promote collaboration with civil society for TB prevention and control. 2.3 Optimize TB data management including surveillance and vital registration.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 21 2.4 Ensure steady supply of anti-TB drugs and laboratory commodities. 2.5 Inclusion of TB in social protection systems, poverty reduction programmes, and action on social determinants of TB. 3. Promote Operational Research and Implementation of Innovative Initiatives and Tools for TB Control Strategic Actions: 3.1 Review new diagnostic tools and medicines. 3.2 Strengthen monitoring and evaluation as a platform for evidence-based programming. 3.3 Implement operational research to generate evidence on the TB situation and for TB control programme. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 24 2.1 Aetiology of Tuberculosis TB is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. These appear as acid-fast bacilli identified using Ziehl Neelson staining. The complex includes Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. africanum which have human reservoirs, and M. bovis from cattle and infected, unpasteurised milk. Other mycobacteria like M. avium complex and M. kansasii can produce disease clinically indistinguishable from tuberculosis. These mycobacteria other than TB (MOTT), can be identified only by culture of the organisms.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 25 2.2 Transmission of Tuberculosis TB in the lungs or throat can be infectious, that is, bacteria can be spread from person to person. TB in other parts of the body such as the kidney or spine is usually not infectious. TB is spread from person to person through the air by droplet nuclei of 1 -5 microns in diameter produced when persons with pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis disease cough, sneeze, speak or sing. These small particles contain the M. tuberculosis complex and depending on the environment may remain suspended in the air for several hours and can be inhaled by the susceptible exposed individual. The smaller particles reach the alveoli within the lung where the organisms replicate. Larger particles do not remain airborne for long and if inhaled do not reach the alveoli but are trapped in mucus and expectorated or swallowed. Tubercle bacilli deposited on intact mucosa or skin does not invade the exposed individual. The likelihood of transmission of M. tuberculosis complex is determined by: 1. The number of organisms being expelled into the air 2. The volume of space and the ventilation 3. The length of time an exposed individual breathes the contaminated air 4. The immune status of the exposed individual

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 26 2.3 Pathogenesis of Tuberculosis After inhalation, the droplet nucleus implants in the alveolus. It multiplies within the alveolar macrophage, growing slowly and producing no immediate host response. The organisms grow for 2 to 12 weeks until they reach numbers which will elicit a cellular immune response that can be detected by a reaction to the tuberculin skin test (TST). Multiplication of the tubercle bacillus takes place in the alveoli, giving rise to an infection known as the Ghon focus, which is a primary lesion caused by tubercle bacilli in the lungs. It is a small area of granulomatous inflammation, only detectable by chest X-ray (CXR) if it calcifies or grows substantially; typically, these will heal. Before the development of cellular immunity tubercle bacilli spread via the lymphatics to the ipsilateral lymph nodes and then through the bloodstream to more distant sites. The Ghon focus, with associated hilar adenopathy is known as the Ghon complex. In persons with intact cellular immunity, collections of activated T cells and macrophages form granulomas that limit multiplication and spread of the organism. However, the bacilli may remain dormant for years. At this stage the majority of pulmonary tuberculosis infections are clinically and radiographically undetectable. A positive tuberculin skin test being the only indication that infection with M. tuberculosis has taken place. Individuals with latent tuberculosis infection but no active disease are not infectious and cannot transmit the organism. Ten percent (10%) of immunocompetent hosts with tuberculosis infection will progress to disease. Fifty percent (50%) of these cases occur 1-2 years after infection. Risk factors for progression from infection to TB disease There are certain conditions that reduce the ability of the individual to respond to the pathogen. These include host factors:  Prior history of active TB, particularly in cases of inadequate treatment  Children under 5 years of age and the elderly  Substance abuse (illicit drugs and alcohol)  Tobacco smoking Medical conditions which increase risk include:  HIV co-infection  Silicosis  Diabetes mellitus  Severe liver disease  Chronic renal failure  Solid organ transplantation  Gastrectomy or jejunoileal bypass

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 27  Certain types of cancer such as leukemia and Hodgkin’s disease  Malnutrition or low body weight (<10% below normal) The use of immunosuppressive drugs is also a risk factor. These include:  Corticosteroids for more than 4 weeks in doses >15mg  Cancer chemotherapy drugs HIV infected persons especially those with low CD4 cell counts develop tuberculosis disease rapidly after becoming infected with M. tuberculosis; up to 50% of such persons do so within 2 years of infection. Those individuals with latent tuberculosis who acquire HIV infection will develop tuberculosis at a rate of 5-10% per year. There is also a higher likelihood of haematogenous spread and disseminated disease.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 28 2.4 Clinical Features The clinical presentation of tuberculosis is quite variable. There are two major types of tuberculosis: pulmonary (85%) and extra-pulmonary (15%). Pulmonary Tuberculosis Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB involving the lung parenchyma or the tracheobronchial tree. Miliary TB is classified as PTB because there are lesions in the lungs. Tuberculous intra-thoracic lymphadenopathy (mediastinal and/or hilar) or tuberculous pleural effusion, without radiographic abnormalities in the lungs, constitutes a case of extra-pulmonary TB. A patient with both pulmonary and extra-pulmonary TB should be classified as a case of PTB (World Health Organization [WHO], 2014). Pulmonary infection is most often manifested by:  Chronic cough (> 2 weeks): non-productive in early disease, but producing sputum as inflammation and tissue necrosis occur  Haemoptysis is usually the result of previous disease  Chest pain may result from pleuritic pain  Dyspnea is usually only found in extensive disease Physical findings are non-specific, with occasional crackles in the area of involvement and bronchial breath sounds if there is lung consolidation. Extra-Pulmonary Tuberculosis Extra-pulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB involving organs (World Health Organization, 2014) other than the lungs, e.g. lymph nodes, pleura, genitourinary tract, skeletal, central nervous system, abdomen, pericardium and skin (WHO, 2014). Extra-pulmonary tuberculosis is more difficult to diagnose than pulmonary tuberculosis, because it is less common and involves relatively inaccessible sites, where fewer bacilli can cause much greater damage. Tuberculosis involving any site may produce symptoms and signs that are not specifically related to the organ or tissue involved, but rather which are systemic in nature. These symptoms and signs include:  Fever  Anorexia  Weight loss  Malaise

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 29  Night sweats  Lymph Node Tuberculosis Tuberculous lymphadenitis usually presents as painless swelling of one or more lymph nodes. The nodes most commonly involved are those of the posterior or anterior cervical chain or supraclavicular fossa. The nodes are initially discrete and overlying skin is normal. With continuing disease, the nodes may become matted and overlying skin inflamed. Intrathoracic nodal involvement may compress bronchi causing atelectasis and lung infection with bronchiectasis. This manifestation is common in children.  Pleural Tuberculosis This commonly goes unnoticed and resolves spontaneously. In some patients, pleural tuberculosis is manifested as an acute illness with fever and pleuritic pain. If there is a large effusion, dyspnea may occur. Pulmonary disease is nearly always present. Involvement of the pleura may also result from rupture of an adjacent cavity, and may lead to emphysema.  Genitourinary Tract Tuberculosis Local symptoms predominate. These include dysuria, haematuria, frequency of urination, and flank pain. However, symptoms may be subtle and there may be advanced destruction of kidneys by the time a diagnosis is made. In women, pelvic pain, menstrual irregularities and infertility may be the presenting complaints of genital involvement. In men a slightly painful scrotal mass is the most common presenting symptom of genital involvement, but symptoms of prostatitis, orchitis and epididymitis may occur. Many patients are asymptomatic and detected through an abnormal urinalysis, which may show pyuria or haematuria.  Skeletal Tuberculosis This usually presents with pain. Swelling of the joints may be noted, associated with limitation of movement and sinus tract formation. Skeletal tuberculosis is more common in children than in adults. Computerised Tomography (CT) scan and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) are more sensitive than routine films. A bone biopsy may be needed to obtain diagnostic material.  Central Nervous System (CNS) Tuberculosis Tuberculous meningitis can result from direct seeding or an old para-meningeal focus with rupture into the subarachnoid space. The process is located primarily at the base of the brain leading to cranial nerve involvement, headache, decreased

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 30 level of consciousness and neck stiffness. This is usually investigated by lumbar puncture, CT scan or MRI.  Abdominal Tuberculosis This may occur in any abdominal organ as well as the peritoneum; clinical manifestations depend on the areas of involvement. The most common sites are the terminal ileum and caecum where it may cause pain and intestinal obstruction. A palpable mass and abnormal barium enema may be mistaken for carcinoma. Rectal lesions may present as fissures, fistulae or abscesses. Tuberculous peritonitis frequently causes pain as its presenting manifestation, accompanied by abdominal swelling, ascites and fever.  Pericardial Tuberculosis This may cause pain, effusion, and haemodynamic effects. The systemic symptoms are non-specific. Cough, dyspnea, orthopnea, ankle swelling and chest pain tend to occur later.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 31 2.5 Diagnosis Figure 2.5.1 shows the clinical algorithm for the investigation and diagnosis of tuberculosis. Any person presenting with a cough of more than 2 weeks duration should be investigated for tuberculosis. Figure 2.5.1: Clinical Algorithm for the Investigation and Diagnosis of Tuberculosis

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 32 This investigation consists of the following: 1. A history and physical examination with a focus on:  Exposure to a person who has infectious TB  Symptoms of TB  Past TB infection or disease  Risk factors/Co-morbid conditions 2. The tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) is usually positive This is performed by injecting 0.1 ml of 5 tuberculin units (TU) of purified protein derivative (PPD) intra-dermally, usually on the forearm. The skin is stretched with the thumb, needle inserted with line and bevel outwards, keeping the needle almost parallel to the skin, the needle is pushed 2-3mm and PPD injected. A blanched wheal should appear in which the skin follicles are readily discernible. The patient's arm is examined 48 to 72 hours later for induration. The diameter of the indurated area across the forearm is measured. The area of erythema around the induration does not indicate infection and should not be measured. The TST may be interpreted as follows:  An induration ≥ 5 mm is classified as positive in the following groups: - Immunosuppressive conditions, HIV, drugs (e.g. chemotherapeutic agents, etc. - Radiographic evidence of active or previously active TB  A tuberculin reaction of ≥ 10 mm of induration is classified as positive in persons who have other risk factors for TB including: - Recent arrivals from high prevalence countries - Frequent exposure to high risk individuals - Residents and employees of high risk congregate settings: prisons, nursing homes etc. - Children under 4 years of age - Medical conditions such as lymphoma, diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure and malnutrition - Recent contacts of persons diagnosed with TB  A tuberculin reaction of ≥ 15 mm of induration is classified as positive in persons:  With no known risk of TB  Age 4 years and older. Persons who have received BCG vaccine are likely to have an induration ≥ 10 mm if tested less than 15 years after vaccination. If BCG vaccination was given more than 15 years previously, it should be ignored as a cause of a current positive skin

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 33 test result especially if the induration is greater than 15mm. Large or strongly positive skin tests are most probably due to TB infection rather than BCG. 3. Bacteriological Investigation Sputum or specimen appropriate to the affected site should be collected and transferred to the TB Laboratory at the National Public Health Laboratory (NPHL). 4. Radiological Investigation Chest X-ray should be done on all patients. There are no chest x-ray findings that are pathognomonic for tuberculosis. There are varying findings such as: cavitary disease, consolidation, pleural effusions, and fibrotic changes. A high index of suspicion must be maintained. 5. HIV Testing An HIV test must be done on each patient at the time of TB diagnosis. Patients with documentary evidence of confirmed HIV infection are exempted, but should be counted among TB patients tested for HIV.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 34 2.6 Classification of Persons Exposed to or Infected with Mycobacterium Tuberculosis 1. No tuberculosis exposure: not infected. There is no history of exposure and a negative tuberculin skin test. 2. Tuberculosis exposure: no evidence of infection. There is a history of exposure, but a negative reaction to the skin test. A follow up test should be done 6 to 8 weeks after the last exposure. 3. Latent tuberculosis: no active disease. There is a positive skin test; negative radiographic, bacteriological and clinical findings. Treatment may be indicated for some persons in this group. The person may have had a previous episode of tuberculosis, or an abnormal radiographic finding and now has a positive skin test, but no other evidence of disease. These persons may never have received chemotherapy, or may be receiving treatment, or may have completed a course of chemotherapy (See Chapter 6: Latent Tuberculosis Infection). 4. Active tuberculosis: All patients with clinically active tuberculosis whose diagnostic procedures are complete. A person must have clinical, bacteriological and/or radiographic evidence of current tuberculosis. A person remains in this class until the treatment is completed. 5. Presumptive tuberculosis case: A patient who has strong clinical or radiological findings in keeping with TB and are pending laboratory diagnosis. Persons should not remain in this class for more than 3 months. Treatment Standardized treatment regimens exist in keeping with the type and classification of TB being treated. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 36 CHAPTER: III MANAGEMENT OF TUBERCULOSIS IN ADULTS 3.1 Aims of Treatment 3.2 Standardized Treatment Regimen 3.3 Recommended Treatment Regimens for Different Treatment Categories 3.4 Management of Chronic and Multi-Drug-Resistant (MDR-TB) Cases

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 37 3.1 Aims of Treatment The aims of treatment of tuberculosis are:  To prevent death from active TB or its late effects  To cure the patient of TB  To prevent relapse of TB  To decrease TB transmission to others Anti-TB treatment will achieve these aims and prevent the emergence of drug resistant M. Tuberculosis. There are three main properties of anti-tuberculosis drugs: 1. Bactericidal activity 2. Sterilizing activity 3. Ability to prevent resistance The classes of anti-TB drugs are divided into first and second line anti-TB drugs. First line anti-TB drugs are: 1. Isoniazid is bactericidal, killing 90% of the total population of bacilli during the first few days of treatment. 2. Rifampin is bactericidal. 3. Pyrazinamide is bactericidal. 4. Ethambutol is bacteriostatic and used in association with the bactericidal drugs to prevent emergence of resistant bacilli.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 38 3.2 Standardized Treatment Regimen The standard treatment regimen involves the use of four antibiotics Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol (RIPE). The combination therapy has proven to be effective against drug sensitive Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Complex (MTBC). Monotherapy is contraindicated. Table 3.2.1 shows the daily dose and dosage range for anti-TB first line drugs used locally. Tuberculosis Treatment Regimens The treatment of Tuberculosis has an intensive phase lasting a minimum of 2 months and a continuation phase lasting 4-6 months. Intensive or Initial Stage During the intensive phase, treatment consists of the four drugs RIPE. Many patients will become non-infectious within two weeks and sputum smear positive TB become smear negative within 6-8 weeks. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is essential during treatment. This improves compliance and helps to prevent drug resistance.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 39 Continuation or Consolidation Stage During the continuation phase, usually only rifampin and isoniazid are required. Directly observed therapy should be continued during the consolidation phase. The recommendation is for daily directly observed therapy (DOT).

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 41 Women on oral contraceptives Rifampin interacts with the oral contraceptive pill and can decrease efficacy against pregnancy. The contraceptive method should be reviewed by the physician. HIV infection All suspected or confirmed TB patients should be tested for HIV infection after receiving appropriate counseling. The standard anti-TB regimen will have to be modified depending on the ARV therapy and the severity of the disease in patients with HIV. Specialist referral will be needed. Patients with liver disorders Patients with hepatitis virus carriage, a past history of acute hepatitis, or excessive alcohol consumption can receive the standard anti-TB regimens provided that there is no clinical evidence of chronic liver disease. These patients need to be monitored closely. Clinical monitoring and liver function tests should be performed during treatment in all patients with pre-existing liver disease. Expert consultation should be sought when treating TB patients with advanced or unstable liver disease. Established chronic liver disease Patients with liver disease-should not receive pyrazinamide. The recommended regimens are the following: 1) Initial phase of 2-months daily SRIE followed by 6 months daily IR; or 2) 2-months daily SIE followed by 10 months daily IE. Specialist referral will be needed. Acute hepatitis (e.g. acute viral hepatitis) In cases where it is necessary to treat TB during acute hepatitis that is unrelated to TB or anti TB treatment, the combination of streptomycin and ethambutol up to a maximum duration of 3 months is the safest option until the hepatitis has resolved. The patient can then receive a continuation phase of 6 months isoniazid and rifampin. Clinical judgment is necessary to determine if TB treatment should be given or deferred until hepatitis has resolved. Patients with renal failure Isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide can be given in the normal dosage to patients with renal failure; these drugs are either eliminated almost entirely by biliary excretion or metabolized into non-toxic compounds. Ethambutol is excreted by the kidney and should be avoided. The recommended regimen to be administered to patients with renal failure

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 42 is 2 months daily IRP followed by 6 months daily IR. In severe renal failure, patients should receive pyridoxine with isoniazid in order to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Six-month treatment regimen Intensive phase - 2 months - Rifampin Isoniazid Pyrazinamide Ethambutol Continuation phase- confirm sputum negativity - Rifampin Isoniazid Interim reports as detailed in the Case Investigation Form (Appendix I) must be sent to the relevant public health department (Medical Officer of Health) at the end of the intensive and continuation phases.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 43 3.4 Management of Chronic and Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Cases are classified as detailed below based on drug susceptibility testing (DST) of clinical isolates confirmed to be M. Tuberculosis. These categories are not mutually exclusive.  Mono-resistance: M. tuberculosis found to be resistant to one of the first line anti- tuberculosis (ATT) drugs only.  Poly-resistance: Bacteria are resistant to more than one of the ATT drugs (other than both isoniazid and rifampin).  Multidrug resistant TB (MDR-TB): Bacteria resistant to at least both isoniazid and Rifampin.  Extensive drug resistant TB (XDR-TB): Resistance to any fluoroquinolone and to at least one of three second line injectable drugs (capreomycin, kanamycin and amikacin) in addition to multi-drug resistance.  Rifampin resistance: Resistance to rifampin detected using phenotypic or genotypic methods, with or without resistance to other anti-TB drugs. It includes any resistance to rifampin, whether mono-resistance, multidrug resistance, polydrug resistance or extensive drug resistance. Background MDR-TB is rarely observed in new cases. The risk is increased and is more frequent in re-treatment cases, especially in failure cases. The aims of treatment in MDR-TB cases are similar to those of all cases with TB. However, MDR-TB patients respond poorly to short-course chemotherapy and need to be treated intensely and for up to 24 months with a regimen based on second line anti-tuberculosis drugs. Full implementation of directly observed therapy DOT (Chapter 9) is the best prevention against MDR-TB. Managerial Principles Management of MDR- TB cases should be carried out by the specialist institution (NCH) and cases must be isolated. The main priority for MDR-TB control is the identification and cure of sputum smear- positive cases. The decision to use second line anti-tuberculosis drugs should be based on:  The availability of financial resources  Laboratories that can perform high-quality drug susceptibility testing  Prevention of uncontrolled use of second line drugs

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 44  Special notification and registration of chronic and MDR-TB cases  Convening of expert committee(s) for decisions on treatment and monitoring. (Proposed membership of this committee to include National Chest Hospital (NCH) Consultant/SMO, NTP Manager, Pulmonologist, Paediatrician, Infectious Disease Consultant, MOHW Epidemiologist, Pharmacist and PAHO Technical Advisor) Treatment of MDR-TB cases with second line drugs is more expensive and more toxic than treatment with essential drugs. Hospitalization entails increased risk of nosocomial transmission of MDR-TB to both staff and patients, especially those infected with HIV. After tolerance of the drug regimen has been ascertained and the patient's cooperation has been secured, the patient can be started on ambulatory treatment. Ambulatory treatment reduces the risk of MDR-TB transmission in hospitals. Management of MDR-TB cases with second line drugs can be done using standardized or individualized regimens. These will be determined based on the recommendations of the expert committee. Special efforts are needed to persuade patients to complete the long treatment regimens required. The advantages of individualized regimens include treatment according to the susceptibility pattern and, likely, higher cure rates. This approach may, however, be costlier than standardized regimens in terms of the drugs involved, in laboratory capability and in the training required to administer a variety of treatment regimens. Standardized treatment regimens have been proven to be successful and are useful in settings where second line drugs have not been used extensively and hence resistances to these drugs are low. Principles of Treatment The treatment regimen should include at least 4 drugs, including an injectable agent and a fluoroquinolone in the initial phase, and at least 3 of the most active and best-tolerated drugs in the continuation phase. An initial phase of at least 6 months should be followed by a continuation phase of 12-18 months. Samples that require drug susceptibility testing should be routed through the NPHL which can liaise with international laboratories. Reserve Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Second line drugs are most useful for the management of MDR-TB cases. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 46 In December 2019, the World Health Organization disseminated the document Rapid Communication: Key changes to the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis (WHO, 2019). Key points from this document are:  All patients with MDR/RR-TB, including those with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones, stand to benefit from effective all-oral treatment regimens, either shorter or longer, implemented under programmatic conditions.  Decisions on appropriate regimens should be made according to patient preference and clinical judgement, also considering the results of susceptibility testing, patient treatment history and severity and site of the disease.  For MDR/RR-TB patients without previous exposure to second-line treatment (including bedaquiline), without fluoroquinolone resistance and no extensive TB disease or severe extrapulmonary TB, the preferred treatment option is a shorter, all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen. Access to rapid drug susceptibility testing, especially for ruling out fluroquinolone resistance is required before starting the shorter, all-oral, bedaquline-containing MDR-TB regimen. Bedaquiline is a bactericidal drug which belongs to a new class of antibiotics (diarylquinolines). The mechanism of action is by interference with the function of an enzyme required by the tuberculosis bacterium to produce energy and to replicate. Currently bedaquiline is not used in Jamaica. The NTP will determine the transition to this treatment regimen in the local context and update the national guidelines as necessary. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 48 CHAPTER: IV MANAGEMENT OF TUBERCULOSIS IN CHILDREN 4.1 Pathogenesis of TB in Children 4.2 Clinical Features 4.3 WHO Case Definitions 4.4 Diagnosis of TB Disease in Children 4.5 Standardized Treatment Regimen 4.6 Special Populations 4.7 Breastfeeding Women 4.8 BCG Vaccine

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 49 4.1 Pathogenesis of TB in Children Infection with M. tuberculosis complex usually results from inhalation into the lungs of aerosolized infected droplets produced by someone who has pulmonary or laryngeal TB. The source of infection of most children is an infectious adult in their close environment (usually the household). This exposure leads to the development of a primary parenchyma lesion (Ghon focus) in the lung with spreading to the regional lymph node(s). The immune response (delayed hypersensitivity and cellular immunity) develops about 4-12 weeks after the primary infection. In most cases, the immune response stops the multiplication of M. tuberculosis bacilli at this stage. However, a few dormant bacilli may persist. A positive tuberculin skin test (TST) would be the only evidence of infection. Disease occurs when the immune response is not strong enough to contain the infection. Inhaled bacteria which are not destroyed result in a primary infection consisting of a small parenchymal focus which spreads locally to regional lymph nodes. The risk of disease progression follows a bimodal pattern as shown in Figure 4.1.1. Infants and young children under age 4 years have the highest propensity to progress to active, disseminated disease due to the age related deficiencies of key immunologic factors. Children aged 5-10 years have the lowest risk of progressive disease while adolescents carry higher risks, including reactivation of M. tuberculosis manifesting as active disease after years of successful containment. Figure 4.1.1: Bimodal Pattern of TB Disease in Children Complications of primary infection occur when:  Parenchymal lesions enlarge or caseate, or nodes enlarge, compress or erode through a bronchus causing wheezing, segmental pneumonia or atelectasis.  Occult or subclinical bacteremia seed distant sites, leading to severe forms such as miliary and CNS TB, particularly in children under age 5 years. Children who develop primary TB usually do so within 2 years following exposure and infection, 90% by the first year. A small proportion of children with TB (usually

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 50 adolescents) develop post-primary TB either due to reactivation, after a latent period of dormant bacilli acquired from a primary infection or by re-infection. M. tuberculosis is capable of infecting nearly any organ. However, the most common clinical manifestations of disease are found within the thoracic cavity and peripheral lymph nodes. Common intrathoracic manifestations include mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy and pulmonary parenchymal lesions. Less commonly, the pleura or pericardium become involved. Extra-thoracic manifestations are common in children and make up approximately 20 - 40% of TB cases. The most commonly involved extra-thoracic sites are the peripheral lymph nodes or the central nervous system. Disease within the central nervous system represents the most serious complication of TB, with significant morbidity or mortality occurring in approximately 50% of cases. Other extra-pulmonary sites include larynx, lymph nodes, pleura, bones, joint, skin, middle ear and mastoid. Gastrointestinal TB can mimic inflammatory bowel disease. Renal TB is unusual in younger children but can occur in adolescents. Clinical Epidemiology Key Points  Most cases occur in young children (<5 years).  Most disease occurs within 2 years after exposure/infection – the majority within 1 year.  Most cases in children are pulmonary TB – Smear negative or smear not done are the majority.  Extra-pulmonary TB is also common and the type depends on age.  Smear positive disease is usually in older children.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 51 4.2 Clinical Features Systemic symptoms and signs that are not specifically related to the organ or tissue involved include:  Fever  Anorexia  Weight loss  Failure to thrive  Malaise  Night sweats Pulmonary infection is most often manifested by: 1. Chronic cough for > 2 weeks without improvement following other appropriate therapies such as broad spectrum antibiotics or treatment for malnutrition 2. Weight loss or failure to gain weight 3. Fever and/or night sweats 4. Fatigue, reduced playfulness, decreased activity Extra-pulmonary TB is common in children and presentation varies with age as shown in Appendix II. Symptoms vary depending on site of disease, and characteristically are persistent, progressive and may be associated with weight loss or poor weight gain. Other signs that may be associated with TB in children include persistent lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and pallor secondary to anaemia.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 52 4.3 WHO Case Definitions The diagnosis of TB refers to the recognition of an active case, i.e. a patient with symptomatic disease (due to M. tuberculosis infection). Similarly, to adults, the type of TB disease should also be defined to enable appropriate treatment to be given and the outcome of treatment evaluated. The case definition is determined by the:  Site of disease  Result of any bacteriological tests  Severity of TB  History of previous anti-TB treatment Tuberculosis is a Class 1 notifiable disease and all children with TB should be notified as detailed in Chapter 7. Tuberculosis in children may be classified as smear-positive pulmonary TB, smear- negative pulmonary TB or extra-pulmonary TB; and as a new case or a previously treated case. Standard case definitions are provided below. WHO also recommends that all cases of childhood TB should be registered and reported within age bands: 0-4 years and 5-14 years. Smear Positive Pulmonary TB To be classified as smear positive pulmonary TB, one of the following criteria must be present:  Two or more initial sputum smear examinations positive for acid-fast bacilli  One sputum smear examination positive for acid-fast bacilli plus CXR abnormalities consistent with active pulmonary TB, as determined by a clinician  One sputum smear examination positive for acid-fast bacilli plus· sputum culture positive for M. tuberculosis Adolescents, or children of any age with complicated intrathoracic disease, are more likely to have sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB. Smear Negative Pulmonary TB Many children are unable to produce sputum and are therefore classified as pulmonary TB smear negative. Diagnostic criteria for sputum smear- negative pulmonary TB should include:  At least three sputum specimens negative for acid-fast bacilli  Radiological abnormalities consistent with active pulmonary TB

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 53  No response to a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics  Decision by a clinician to treat with a full course of anti-TB chemotherapy Extra-pulmonary TB Children with only extra-pulmonary TB should be classified under this case definition. Those who have both pulmonary and extra-pulmonary TB should be classified as pulmonary TB. Drug Resistant TB Drug resistant TB can occur in children. Drug-resistant TB should be suspected if there is a history in the index case of:  Exposure to a known case of drug-resistant TB  Sputum remains smear-positive after 3 months of treatment  History of previously treated TB  History of treatment interruption Features of a child suspected of having drug-resistant TB:  Contact with a known case of drug-resistant TB  Not responding to the anti-TB treatment regimen  Recurrence of TB after adherence to treatment The diagnosis and treatment of drug-resistant TB in children is complex and should be carried out at the Bustamante Hospital for Children, the paediatric referral hospital.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 54 4.4 Diagnosis of TB Disease in Children An accurate diagnostic test for paediatric TB does not exist. TB in children is often a clinical diagnosis and, a negative test does not rule out disease in children. Approach to diagnosis: 1. Medical history 2. Clinical examination including growth assessment 3. Tuberculin skin test 4. Bacteriological confirmation whenever possible 5. Investigations relevant for suspected PTB or suspected EPTB 6. HIV testing 1. Medical History The history includes social, family and medical information on the patient:  History of exposure to a person who has infectious TB  Symptoms of TB  Past TB infection or disease  Risk factors  Contact history: - Closeness of contact - Sputum smear result of index case (if known) - Timing of contact, children usually develop TB within 2 years after exposure and most (90%) within the first year - If no index case is identified, always ask about anyone in household with cough and request assessment of that person for possible TB - 2. Clinical Examination There are no specific features on clinical examination that can confirm pulmonary TB. Common signs that should prompt an investigation into the possibility of childhood TB are shown in Table 4.4.1.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 55 Table 4.4.1: Clinical Features of Paediatric Tuberculosis Pulmonary Extra-pulmonary Systemic Dull percussion note Gibbus (vertebral TB) Weight loss or failure to thrive Crepitations Enlarged lymph nodes Fever Decreased or absent breath sounds Meningitis not responding to antibiotic treatment Lethargy Pleural effusion Pericardial effusion Distended abdomen with ascites Non-painful enlarged joint Signs of tuberculin hypersensitivity (e.g. phlyctenular conjunctivitis, erythema nodosum The TST can also be used as an adjunct in diagnosing TB in children with signs and symptoms of TB. 3. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) A positive TST occurs when a person is infected with M. tuberculosis, but does not necessarily indicate disease. However, the TST can also be used as an adjunct in diagnosing TB in children with signs and symptoms of TB. A TST should be regarded as positive, whether they have received a Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccination or not, under the following circumstances: i. Induration 5 mm diameter or greater  Children in close contact with a known or suspected contagious person with tuberculosis disease  Children suspected to have tuberculous disease (clinical and /or radiological findings)  Children with immunosuppressive conditions (e.g. HIV infected, on immunosuppressive therapy) ii. Induration 10 mm or greater  Children at increased risk of disseminated tuberculous disease (Children younger than 4 years or children with other medical conditions such as Hodgkin’s disease, lymphoma, diabetes, chronic renal failure, malnutrition)

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 56  Children with a likelihood of increased exposure to tuberculous disease (e.g. children frequently exposed to adults who are HIV infected, homeless, users of illicit drugs, residents of nursing homes, incarcerated or institutionalized iii. Induration 15 mm or greater  Children age 4 years or older without any risk factors Value of the TST in children  The TST can be used to screen children exposed to TB (such as from household contact with TB), though children can still receive chemoprophylaxis even if the TST is not available.  Due to the high risk of progression to severe forms of TB in the under 5 age group, the identification, screening and treatment of Latent TB Infection and active TB disease in potential adult and adolescent contacts is paramount in protecting this vulnerable group.  The TST is useful in HIV-infected children to identify those with dual TB/HIV although immunosuppressed children may have a negative TST.  A negative test does not exclude disease and a positive test does not differentiate latent TB Infection from active TB disease. 4. Bacteriological Confirmation A bacteriological specimen must be collected on initial examination. Bacteriological confirmation is ideal. Common ways of obtaining samples for smear microscopy include the following: a. Expectoration In children under 5 years of age, sputum is difficult to obtain. However, in children who are able to produce a specimen, it should be collected for bacteriological confirmation. Older children (10 years of age or older) are usually able to provide a sputum sample. Three sputum specimens should be obtained:  An on-the-spot specimen (at first evaluation)  An early morning specimen  A second on-the-spot specimen (at a follow-up visit). The procedure for sputum specimen collection, handling and transfer is detailed in Chapter 8.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 57 b. Gastric aspiration Gastric aspiration using a nasogastric feeding tube can be performed in young children who are unable to expectorate sputum. A gastric aspirate should be obtained on three consecutive mornings.  Patients should have nil per os (NPO) for eight hours prior to the procedure.  Aspirate the stomach contents first. Then instil no more than 50 ml of sterile distilled water. Aspirate the contents of the stomach and add the aspirate as the first specimen.  The specimen should be delivered to the laboratory within 4 hours of collection because acid is detrimental to mycobacteria. If that is not possible, it should be directly placed into a buffered solution (refer to Chapter 8). c. Sputum induction Sputum induction is safe and effective in children of all ages and the bacterial yields are as good as or better than for gastric aspirates. However, training and specialized equipment are required to perform this procedure properly. Patients should be kept NPO for eight hours before the procedure. The sputum induction procedure can be administered by a physiotherapist using 4 steps:  Administration of salbutamol.  Delivery of hypertonic saline by nebulizer.  Chest percussion, vibration, or active breathing performed by a trained technician.  Sample collection following spontaneous expectoration or suction of the naso-oropharynx should be obtained on each of three consecutive mornings. 5. Chest X-ray A chest x-ray is an important tool for diagnosing PTB in children. The most common radiological feature is hilar or para-tracheal lymphadenopathy which tends to be asymmetrical. Frontal and lateral chest radiographs are required to detect this. Parenchymal lesions can be anywhere in primary disease. Typically, in adolescents the upper lobes are involved. Infants can present as severe pneumonia with extensive parenchymal disease and respiratory distress that is challenging to

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 58 differentiate from the many other possible causes of pneumonia in infants. Note that a contact history is very important and often positive in infants with TB disease. Cavitation is rare but may be present in very young or immunocompromised children with adult type disease or with caseating pneumonia secondary to lymphobronchial disease. An experienced radiologist should ideally review films. 6. HIV testing As in all cases of TB, an HIV test is mandatory in the assessment of children with TB. Administering treatment and ensuring adherence Children, their parents and other family members, as well as other caregivers, should be educated about TB and the importance of adherence and completing treatment. The support of the child's parents and immediate family is vital to ensuring a satisfactory outcome of treatment. Often a health-care worker can observe or administer treatment, but if this arrangement is not convenient for the family, a trained community member (preferably someone other than the child's parent or immediate family) can undertake this responsibility. All children should receive treatment free of charge, whether the child is smear-positive at diagnosis or not. Fixed-dose combinations of drugs should be used whenever possible to improve simplicity and adherence. Patient treatment cards are recommended for documenting treatment adherence. Specialist management is warranted in cases with: • Severe forms of PTB and EPTB (such as TB meningitis and miliary TB) for further investigation and initial management • Severe malnutrition for nutritional rehabilitation • Signs of severe pneumonia (i.e. chest in-drawing) or respiratory distress • Other co-morbidities e.g. severe anaemia • Severe adverse events, such as clinical signs of hepatotoxicity (e.g. jaundice) • Diagnostic uncertainty requiring further investigation at referral level • Necessary for HIV-related care e.g. to commence ART Children require close clinical monitoring, which should include symptom assessment, weight measurement, assessment of adherence to treatment and enquiry about any

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 59 adverse events. Dosages of anti-TB drugs should be adjusted to account for any weight gain. For the continuation phase, if it is not possible to ensure good adherence and treatment outcome on an outpatient basis, some children may require hospitalization for social or logistical reasons. Chest X-ray (CXR) 2 months into treatment should be done to rule out extension of disease. Persistent radiographic signs are not an indication to change treatment if there is clinical improvement. Residual scarring may persist for 2-3 years. A normal CXR is not necessary to discontinue treatment. Patients should be followed for 1 year after treatment completion to monitor clinical health and resolution of radiographic findings.

Treatment Response Most children with TB, including those who are HIV-infected, have a good response to the 6-month regimen. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 62 4.6 Special Populations  HIV infected children  Adolescents  The exposed child  The exposed newborn HIV Infected Children HIV-infected children are at 20-times greater risk of TB disease than HIV-uninfected children and at much higher risk of TB-related death. Those who are infected with HIV have impaired cell-mediated immunity to control TB infection, conferring a higher risk of progression to active TB disease after exposure; of reactivation of latent infection; and of severe disease manifestations. Timely recognition of HIV and initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is essential for immune restoration and improved TB control. It is recommended that HIV-infected children receive: 1. Four first-line drugs (RIPE) in the intensive phase for suspected or confirmed drug-sensitive TB irrespective of severity of disease 2. Similar duration of regimens as for HIV-uninfected 3. ART as recommended within 2-8 weeks of starting TB treatment or continue ART 4. Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy 5. Pyridoxine supplement 6. Nutritional support Where possible, HIV-infected children should be treated with rifampin for the entire treatment duration, as higher relapse rates among HIV infected adults have been found when ethambutol is used in the continuation phase. There has been caution in the use of ethambutol in children too young to report early visual deterioration, but ethambutol has been safely used in infants and young children at recommended dosages. Children on ethambutol should receive visual assessment before and after treatment. ART regimens for children in need of TB treatment All newly diagnosed TB cases that are also HIV positive and are ARV naïve should be started on TB therapy immediately and initiate ARV treatment within 2 to 8 weeks. HIV positive TB patients with profound immunosuppression (e.g. CD4 counts less than 50

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 63 cells/ mm3) should receive ART within the first two weeks of initiating TB treatment. Table 4.6.1 shows the recommended regimen for children and infants starting ART while on TB treatment. Consider consultation with experts for construction of second-line regimen. Adolescents Adolescence is a uniquely susceptible time for disease progression. Disease presentation can vary from childhood manifestations to adult type TB, with cavitary pulmonary TB or extra-thoracic manifestations with longer incubation periods such as genitourinary TB. Health care workers should inquire about substance abuse, anxiety or depression which may be exacerbated by infection control measures or contact investigation procedures and stigma associated with the disease. Adherence and follow up may be affected by these factors compounded by behavioural aspects of adolescence resulting in poor outcomes. The TB Exposed Child and Management of Contacts A child with tuberculosis represents a sentinel event of ongoing transmission in the community. Prompt evaluation and treatment of children exposed to an infectious adult source is the most efficient way to prevent pulmonary TB.  All exposed children should have a symptom enquiry  Children less than 5 years and symptomatic children should have a physical examination and chest x-ray

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 65 Window therapy  All children less than 5 years with a negative TST and no active disease by examination or radiology should be given “window” preventative therapy to prevent the development of TB  This is because it takes up to 8 weeks after infection for the TST to convert to positive during which time the infection will progress to disease  Isoniazid is used for presumed drug susceptible exposure  Isoniazid may be discontinued if after 8 weeks, after the last contact, the TST is negative, the child remains asymptomatic, is immunocompetent and is greater than 6 months old  For children < 6 months please see management of the newborn exposed to TB In the exposed child, if the TST is positive and there is no clinical or radiographic disease, then a full course of treatment for LTBI is recommended. When a new active child is the index case, vigorous reverse contact tracing should be carried out to find the source case. Most source cases are household contacts but non household contacts such as caregivers should be sought. For patients admitted to hospital, adolescent or adult visitors should be screened for active TB. Congenital Tuberculosis This is a relatively uncommon event but a high index of suspicion must be maintained. Spread occurs via the haematogenous route direct from reproductive organs or postnatally from respiratory transmission. Symptoms are nonspecific and indistinguishable from bacterial sepsis or congenital viral infections and manifest as early as 2-3 weeks of age. Infants born to mothers with active or confirmed TB or LTBI should be managed according to the scenarios in Table 4.6.3. Evaluation of congenital TB includes clinical examination, TST, cultures including lumbar puncture, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasound and cranial ultrasound. The initial TST will be negative but becomes positive 1-3 months after treatment. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 68 4.7 Breast Feeding Women Once a pregnant woman has been on treatment for at least 2-3 weeks, she is generally no longer infectious. If a pregnant woman with TB has been on treatment for TB for several weeks before delivery, it is less likely that the baby will become infected. The risk is highest, if a mother is diagnosed at the time of delivery or shortly thereafter. If a pregnant woman is found to have pulmonary TB shortly before delivery, then the baby, and possibly the placenta should be investigated for evidence of congenital TB infection, and if found, the baby treated.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 69 4.8 BCG Vaccination The HIV pandemic has implications for BCG vaccination. Although there have been a few reports of disseminated BCG disease after BCG immunisation of HIV-infected children, prospective studies comparing BCG immunisation in HIV-infected and uninfected infants have shown no difference in risk of complications. It is recommended that BCG vaccination policy should depend on the prevalence of TB in a country. In countries with a high TB prevalence, the benefits of BCG vaccination outweigh the risks, and WHO recommends a policy of routine BCG immunisation for all neonates. BCG vaccine should not be given to symptomatic HIV infected children because of the risks of disseminated BCG disease. In Jamaica, the National Expanded Programme on lmmunisations recommends routine BCG immunisation in the neonatal period to all infants. Management of BCG disease in HIV-infected children (or children with other immuno-deficiencies) The diagnosis of BCG disease is difficult and the treatment is specialized, as M. bovis is resistant to pyrazinamide and requires higher doses of other first-line TB medications - e.g. some experts recommend a daily dose of isoniazid of up to 15 mg/kg (maximum 300mg) and a daily dose of Rifampin of up to 20 mg/kg (maximum 600 mg). HIV- infected children suspected of having BCG disease should be referred to an appropriate expert for management.
