Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 71 CHAPTER: V HIV/TUBERCULOSIS CO-INFECTION 5.1 Management of TB/HIV Co-Infection

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 72 5.1 HIV/Tuberculosis Co-infection Persons infected with HIV have a greater risk of infection with Tuberculosis and developing active TB. Figure 5.1.1 outlines the clinical algorithm for the diagnosis and management of HIV/Tuberculosis co-infection. All persons infected with HIV must be screened and if indicated tested for TB; and if found to have either latent or active TB must be effectively treated. Conversely, all persons with TB must be tested for HIV and appropriately managed. Figure 5.1.1: Clinical Algorithm for the Investigation and Diagnosis of HIV/Tuberculosis Co-infection

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 73 TB and HIV/AIDS Standards of Treatment and Management 1. Prior to initiating any TB therapy, review all medications that the individual is taking and assess for potential drug interactions with TB medications. 2. In TB/HIV co-infection, initiation of treatment for TB takes precedence over the treatment of HIV and should be commenced first. Persons already on HAART can be continued with appropriate modifications, both in anti-retroviral therapy (ART) and anti TB treatment. 3. In persons who were not previously on ART, the need and timing of ART initiation is decided after assessing the risk of HIV disease progression. 4. Concurrent administration of rifampin with certain HIV medications (ART) may require dose adjustments or switches to alternative ART or anti-tuberculous drugs to reduce both interactions and toxicity. 5. A CD4 count should be obtained. 6. All patients being treated for TB should receive a daily DOT regimen for the entire course of therapy. Do not switch to a two times weekly or three times weekly regimen. (PAHO, 2017) 7. TB drugs should be calculated according to mg/kg body weight. This should be done on the lower figure in the range and rounded up to the next available dose supplied by the manufacturer (For dosage table, see Chapter 3). 8. HIV-positive individuals treated with isoniazid should receive Pyridoxine (B6) 25 mg daily on the same schedule as isoniazid. 9. Ingestion of 9 months of isoniazid or 4 months of rifampin is considered adequate preventive therapy. 10. All HIV/TB patients need to be monitored closely for response to treatment and signs of treatment failure or relapse; if failure or relapse is suspected, assume rifampin resistance until culture-confirmed otherwise. Treatment modification will require consultation with a physician who is an expert in the management of TB. Monitoring a. Pre-treatment evaluation  Do a chest x-ray, symptom review and complete physical examination to exclude active tuberculosis disease. If active disease is excluded, no further chest x-rays are recommended for the patient who remains asymptomatic.  Obtain medical history including: - Previous adverse reaction to any TB drugs - Underlying liver disease - Previous Isoniazid associated liver injury

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 74 - Current medications  Obtain a baseline liver profile and viral hepatitis screen and manage abnormalities as appropriate.  Obtain a baseline CBC including platelets and appropriately manage any abnormalities detected. b. Monitoring during treatment Clinical assessment should be performed on at least a monthly basis for all patients being treated for TB. Patients should be assessed for:  Adherence to the prescribed regimen  Signs and symptoms of adverse drug reactions - If individual is on rifampin - at each visit evaluate for potential interactions with HIV drugs or any other medication. - Monthly lab monitoring, done at baseline and at the end of the first two months of therapy, thereafter symptom driven or as indicated. - Manage individuals with asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations, adverse reactions or hepatoxicity. Tuberculosis Disease in Patients with HIV/AIDS The treatment regimen in HIV/AIDS patients may involve different TB drugs, daily dosing and may require a longer treatment duration. 1. Drugs used to treat TB in HIV/AIDS adults ≥ 15 yrs. a. If the patient is on antiretroviral therapy, the patient's TB treatment regimen should be reviewed with a specialist physician. b. Individuals should receive the usual 4-drug TB regimen (Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol) if they are not on antiretroviral therapy or on NRTI- class drugs (e.g. Zidovudine) and NNRTIs (e.g. Efavirenz or Nevirapine). 2. Individuals receiving any other antiretroviral will need to have Rifabutin (RBT) substituted for Rifampin; this should be done in consultation with a physician knowledgeable about treating HIV/AIDS and TB. a. Monitoring of patients taking Rifabutin should include complete blood count looking for neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; the patient should also be asked about uveitis (eye pain, visual changes). b. Other drugs, for example clarithromycin and fluconazole can increase RBT levels and cause RBT toxicity.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 75 3. When switching from a rifampin based regimen to a RBT or non-rifampin based regimen, wait at least 2 weeks before initiating antiretroviral drugs to prevent the interference of rifampin with the antiretroviral drug. 4. Individuals who are unable to take a Rifampin or Rifabutin-based regimen, should be managed as follows using DOTs: a. Individuals on an initial regimen of Isoniazid, Rifampin/Rifabutin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol:  Discontinue Rifampin/Rifabutin; discontinue Pyrazinamide after 2 months and continue to treat with Isoniazid and Ethambutol for a total of 18 months. OR  Discontinue Rifampin; add Streptomycin and continue to treat with Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol and Streptomycin for 2 months. Discontinue Ethambutol after 2 months and continue to treat with Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide and Streptomycin for 7 months.  If Streptomycin cannot be given for the total duration of treatment or for at least 4 months following culture conversion, add Ethambutol back into the regimen and treat for a total of 12 months. 5. Therapeutic drug monitoring is suggested for patients with risk factors for altered drug absorption or metabolism and excretion. This includes: a. Gastrointestinal disease or HIV infection, due to the potential of malabsorption of drugs. b. Liver or renal disease, due to reduced drug excretion. c. Drug resistant TB disease, to allow optimal availability of all drugs 6. Duration of treatment a. The minimum duration of short-course rifampin or Rifabutin-containing TB regimens is 26 weeks. b. If Pyrazinamide is not started within the first 2 weeks of treatment and continued for the first 8 weeks of therapy, or if Pyrazinamide is contraindicated, a minimum of nine months of Isoniazid and Rifampin is required and the first 8 weeks of treatment must be administered daily by DOT. c. If at the end of 8 weeks of therapy, the individual does not experience resolution of symptoms of TB, or if their sputum culture does not convert to negative, treat for a total of 9 months, to include a minimum of 4 months after documented culture conversion.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 76 7. Patients with HIV/TB coinfection should also receive co-trimoxazole as prophylaxis. Consideration for continuation after TB treatment is completed is in accordance with HIV national treatment guidelines. 8. Regimens for Pregnant Women a. The only difference between treating HIV-positive and HIV-negative pregnant women is the use of Pyrazinamide. The benefit of optimal treatment of TB in HIV- positive pregnant women outweighs the very small risk of using Pyrazinamide in pregnancy. Therefore, for HIV/AIDS and TB in pregnant women, follow the treatment recommendations above. b. Streptomycin is contraindicated for pregnant women 9. Regimens for Infants and Children <15 yr. a. Standard TB therapy of Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol with daily DOT is given for eight weeks.  Discontinue Ethambutol when initial culture results confirm the organisms are fully susceptible to Isoniazid and Rifampin.  Discontinue Pyrazinamide after 8 weeks.  If susceptibility results are not done or unknown, give Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol followed by Isoniazid and Rifampin for 18 weeks.  Individuals too young to have visual acuity or red-green perception testing should receive Ethambutol at a dosage of 15-mg/kg body weight, or Ethambutol may be omitted at the discretion of the prescribing physician. b. Due to the interaction with Rifampin, individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy should have a consultation with a HIV/TB clinical specialist. c. Infants and children with meningeal, bone, joint or miliary TB should receive a minimum of 12 months of therapy. 10. Regimens for Extra-pulmonary TB a. Individuals with TB at any site should have a chest x-ray and if able to produce sputum, a sputum specimen for smear or culture. b. Adults with meningeal, bone and joint TB should be treated for a minimum of 9 months, and may be extended to12 months total. All other sites should be treated with the same drug regimens recommended for pulmonary TB. 11. Regimens for Isoniazid Resistance or Intolerance a. Individuals on initial regimen of Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol:  Discontinue Isoniazid; continue to treat with Rifampin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol for a total of 6 months or 4 months after documented culture conversion, whichever is longer.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 77 OR  Discontinue Isoniazid and Pyrazinamide; continue to treat with Rifampin and Ethambutol for minimum of 12 months. b. Individuals on an initial regimen of Isoniazid, Rifampin and Ethambutol:  Discontinue Isoniazid; continue to treat with Rifampin and Ethambutol for a minimum of 12 months. 12. Regimens for Rifampin Resistance or Intolerance a. Individuals on initial regimen of Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol:  Discontinue Rifampin; discontinue Pyrazinamide after 2 months and continue to treat with Isoniazid and Ethambutol for a total of 18 months. OR  Discontinue Rifampin; add Streptomycin and continue to treat with Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol and Streptomycin for 2 months. Discontinue Ethambutol after 2 months and continue to treat with Isoniazid, Streptomycin and Pyrazinamide for 7 months. - If Streptomycin cannot be given for the total duration of treatment or for at least 4 months following culture conversion, add Ethambutol back into the regimen and treat for a total of 12 months. 13. Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB)  MDR-TB is TB resistant to both Isoniazid and Rifampin.  Treatment must be individualized and prolonged based on medication history and susceptibility studies.  Give at least 3 drugs to which the organism is susceptible. The regimen should continue until sputum conversion is documented, followed by at least 12 months of a two-drug therapy.  Consult the TB Consultant. 14. Monitoring is the same as for HIV-negative TB patients. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is an inflammatory reaction that can occur when the immune system of an HIV-positive patient improves with anti- retroviral therapy. In TB/HIV co-infected patients, IRIS may occur in up to 33% of patients and usually occurs within the first three months of starting therapy. IRIS associated with TB may present with fever, appearance of new adenopathies, increased size of pre- existing adenopathy, pain or respiratory symptoms. Management of IRIS includes:

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 78  Treatment of opportunistic infection to reduce the antigenic load  Continuation of ART  Use of anti-inflammatory drugs or corticosteroids Severe reactions may occur which include respiratory failure or tracheal compression due to massive adenopathy. These cases require support and corticosteroid therapy (prednisone 0.5mg/kg/day for five to ten days). (PAHO, 2017) Guideline: HIV/Tuberculosis Co-Infection Date Revised: November 2021 Distribution to hospitals and health centres Index: V Approved by: Senior Medical Officer HIV/STI/TB Unit
Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 79 CHAPTER: VI LATENT TUBERCULOSIS INFECTION

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 80 CHAPTER: VI LATENT TUBERCULOSIS INFECTION 6.1 Latent Tuberculosis 6.2 Who to Test 6.3 Diagnosis of Latent Tuberculosis 6.4 Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 81 6.1 Latent Tuberculosis Latent Tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, with no clinically manifested evidence of active TB disease. Up to one third of the world’s population is estimated to be infected with M. tuberculosis, the majority of which have no signs or symptoms of active TB disease, and although not having active TB disease currently, are still at risk for active TB disease and becoming infectious. The risk of developing active TB disease is approximately 5-10% (WHO, 2015) and usually occurs within the first five years of initial infection. This is dependent on several factors, significantly immunological state. Population wide testing for LTBI is not feasible and not recommended due not only to the cost but also due to unproven public health impact and the risk for drug-related adverse side effects. However, in certain population groups where the risk of progression to active disease is higher, the benefits of treatment outweigh the harm. Management of LTBI involves the following: 1. Identifying and testing those who should be tested 2. Complete safe treatment with minimal or no side effects 3. Monitoring and evaluation of the process

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 82 6.2 Who to Test Preventive treatment of M. tuberculosis infection should be selectively targeted to the population groups at highest risk for progression to active TB disease and would consequently benefit most from treatment of LTBI. Jamaica is classified as an upper middle-income country, as such the following are recommended for at-risk populations for LTBI testing and treatment: 1. Systematic testing and treatment should be performed in: - Persons living with HIV - as per recommendation in Chapter 5 - Contacts of pulmonary TB - both children and adults - Patients initiating anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) treatment - Patients receiving dialysis - Patients preparing for organ or haematologic transplantation - Patients with silicosis 2. Systematic testing and treatment should be considered for: - Prisoners - Health Care workers - Immigrants from high burden TB countries - Homeless persons - Illicit drug users Systematic testing for LTBI is not recommended in people with diabetes, people with harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers and underweight persons unless they are already included in the above recommendations.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 83 6.3 Diagnosis of Latent TB 1. Check for active disease. The clinical algorithm for the investigation and diagnosis of HIV/TB Co-infection (Figure 5.1) should be utilized. However, patients with latent TB are asymptomatic. For active disease patients might not have classical symptoms, and radiographs may not be typical of expected findings; hence clinicians must have a high index of suspicion when dealing with HIV positive patients. 2. Perform tuberculin skin test. a. Indurations of ≥ 5mm are considered positive. Assess further for active versus latent disease using chest radiographs. b. Indurations of <5mm do not rule out the presence of disease. Correlate TST result with clinical presentation. c. For persons whose initial TST was negative and the CD4 count < 200mm3, the TST should be repeated once the CD4 count becomes greater than 200mm3. 3. If the patient had a positive TST, perform a chest X-ray to identify changes associated with TB disease: - HIV/AIDS individuals ≥ 5 years of age should receive a posterior- anterior chest x-ray. - HIV/AIDS individuals < 5 years of age should receive a posterior- anterior and lateral chest x-ray. 4. If no abnormalities are detected on the chest x-ray, the patient should be treated for LTBI. 5. If any abnormality is detected on the chest x-ray, further investigations should be done for TB and or other diseases as indicated. Figure 6.3.1 outlines the algorithm for the targeted diagnosis and treatment of LTBI in individuals from risk groups.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 84 Figure 6.3.1: Algorithm for Targeted Diagnosis and Treatment of LTBI in Individuals from Risk Groups (WHO, 2015) *Symptoms of TB include any one of: cough, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath and fatigue. ** Clients for whom LTBI treatment is not indicated should be provided with information about TB including the importance of seeking care if symptoms of TB develop. ***Follow National TB Guidelines for TB investigation. Additionally, those in whom TB is excluded after investigations (including individuals with fibrotic radiologic lesions) can be considered for LTBI treatment.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 85 6.4 Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Six months daily monotherapy with Isoniazid is the treatment for both adults and children. The recommended treatment option for LTBI is detailed in Table 6.4.1 below (WHO, 2018). Table 6.4.1: Six Month Daily Isoniazid Treatment Regimens for LTBI Drug Regimen Dose per kg body weight Maximum dose Adults (Daily for Six months) Isoniazid 5 mg/kg 300 mg Children (Daily for Six months) Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (range 7 -15mg) 300 mg Alternate regimens to the six months of monotherapy with Isoniazid are detailed in Table 6.4.2 below (WHO, 2018). Table 6.4.2: Alternate Treatment Regimens for LTBI Drug regimen Dose per kg body weight Maximum dose Isoniazid (daily for 6 or 9 months) Adults – 5mg Children – 10mg (range 7 – 15mg) 300mg Daily Rifampin alone for 3 – 4 months Adults – 10mg Children – 15mg (range 10-20mg) 600mg Daily Isoniazid plus Rifampin for 3 -4 months Isoniazid Adults – 5mg Children – 10mg (range 7 – 15mg) Rifampin Adults – 10mg Children – 15mg (range 10-20mg) Isoniazid – 300mg Rifampin – 600mg The patient does not require admission as they are not infectious for TB. They do require follow up in light of adherence at the primary health care setting on a weekly basis. The

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 86 follow up can be done by a Community Health Aide who reports to the Public Health Nurse on the compliance of patient and completion of medication. Isoniazid and Rifampin are both tolerated and recommended for treatment of LTBI in pregnant women and during breast feeding. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 88 CHAPTER: VII TUBERCULOSIS SURVEILLANCE 7.1 Goal and Objectives of Tuberculosis Surveillance 7.2 Case Detection 7.3 Case Definitions 7.4 Case Investigation 7.5 Data Management

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 89 7.1 Goal and Objectives of Tuberculosis Surveillance Tuberculosis surveillance aims to detect and measure the number of TB cases and related deaths that occur each year and to assess trends in these parameters over time. Objectives of TB surveillance 1. Describe the number of new TB cases by category  Multi-Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis  HIV positive (co-infected)  Age/Sex distribution  Geographic distribution 2. Measure the number of TB deaths 3. Track new cases and deaths over time 4. Measure treatment outcome by:  Age/Sex  Classification (pulmonary versus extra-pulmonary)  Time (trends)  Geographic distribution

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 90 7.2 Case Detection Medical Practitioners shall notify as Tuberculosis all patients presenting with a chronic cough (> 3 weeks duration). Tuberculosis is a Class 1 notifiable disease, therefore all suspected cases should be reported within 24 hours to the Parish Health Department or National Surveillance Unit [Public Health (Class 1 Notifiable Diseases) Order 2003, Government of Jamaica, 2003].

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 91 7.3 Case Definitions (WHO, 2013) a) Suspected case – A person who presents with a persistent cough for greater than 3 weeks. b) Confirmed case - Bacteriologically confirmed - Person from whom a biological specimen is positive by smear microscopy, culture or PCR (Such as Xpert MTB/RIF). - Clinically diagnosed case – An individual who does not fulfil the criteria for bacteriological confirmation but has been diagnosed with active TB by a clinician or other medical practitioner who has decided to give the patient a full course of TB treatment. c) Pulmonary TB - A bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB, with disease involving the lung parenchyma or the trachea- bronchial tree. Tuberculous intra-thoracic lymphadenopathy or tuberculous pleural effusion without radiographic evidence of lung lesions is classified as extra-pulmonary TB. A case with pulmonary and extra- pulmonary TB should be classified as a case of pulmonary TB. Miliary TB is classified as pulmonary TB. d) Extra-pulmonary TB - A bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB with disease involving organs other than the lungs and no pulmonary involvement (see pulmonary TB above). e) New patient - A patient with bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed Tuberculosis who has never been treated for TB or who has taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. f) A relapsed patient - A patient who has previously been treated for TB and declared cured or treatment completed and is now diagnosed with TB (Bacteriologically Confirmed or Clinically Diagnosed). Notification of TB Cases by Health Care Workers All suspected cases of Tuberculosis shall be notified using a Class 1 notification form (Appendix III). The notification form must be completed with all available information about the suspected case and transmitted to the Parish Health Department or the National Surveillance Unit within 24 hours of suspicion. The Parish Health Department must

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 92 forward notifications to the Regional Health Authority and the National Surveillance Unit as detailed in the National Surveillance Manual for Jamaica. Hospital Active Surveillance Officers are responsible for searching the wards and laboratory of each hospital for cases of tuberculosis that were not reported as above.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 93 7.4 Case Investigation The responsibility for case investigation lies with the Parish Medical Officer (Health) who will delegate as appropriate. Contact investigation should be carried out for all confirmed cases of TB (bacteriologically and clinically confirmed). The schedule for completing the Case Investigation Form (Appendix I) is as follows:  Sections 1- 4 to be submitted within 2 weeks of receipt of the notification  Section 5 will be completed at the central level (MOHW)  Section 6 should be completed within 6 weeks of the initial notification  Section 7 should be completed when the case has completed treatment  Section 8 to be completed by the MOHW within 6 weeks of completion of treatment  A review of the suspected case’s medical records will be required with special attention paid to the following: o Previous History of TB o Chest X-Ray findings o Mantoux Test result o Sputum sample collection o Sputum results o HIV testing o HIV status o Comorbid conditions (E.g. diabetes, renal disease, etc.) o Treatment History Contact Tracing Contact tracing (WHO, 2012) is a critical component of the case investigation and aims to limit the spread of disease. The investigating officer must: o Identify all household and bedroom contacts (initiated once notification received) o Screen all close contacts as follows:  Take a thorough history from each contact focused on HIV status, other comorbidities, and recent history of cough, weight loss, and night sweats  Conduct a Mantoux test on each household, bedroom, and other close contact  Refer as appropriate for further management  Contacts are prioritized for investigation based on:

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 94 1. Closeness of contact. For example, persons sharing a bedroom and/or a bed with a clinically diagnosed or bacteriologically confirmed individual with Tuberculosis are more likely to become infected. This is not limited to the household but may include homeless shelters and other settings with multi- person ‘wards,’ such as an infirmary or areas of confinement such as prisons or lock ups. 2. Duration of contact. The longer a person spends in close contact with a person suspected or proven to have Tuberculosis (as above), the greater the risk of transmission and infection. 3. Immune status of the contact. A person living with HIV is more likely to progress rapidly to active TB disease once infected. 4. Presence of pulmonary Tuberculosis in the index case (the case around whom the investigation is centered). Transmission of disease is more likely in a person suspected or proven to have Pulmonary Tuberculosis than from a person with Extra-Pulmonary Tuberculosis. 5. Age of the Contact. Children < 5 years old are more likely to develop severe disease. Management of Contacts The management of contacts will depend on the results of initial screening and on the immune status of the contact (Figure 7.4.1).
Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 95 Figure 7.4.1: Algorithm for Screening of Contacts for Active Tuberculosis (WHO 2013)

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 96 7.5 Data Management Collection  A Class 1 form is to be submitted by the medical practitioner to the Parish Health Department or to the National Surveillance Unit within 24 hours of suspicion of a diagnosis of Tuberculosis.  Sections 1 – 4 of the Tuberculosis Case Investigation Form (Appendix I) are to be completed and submitted within 2 weeks of notification.  Section 5 will be completed at the central level (MOHW).  Section 6 of the Tuberculosis Case Investigation Form should be completed within 6 weeks of the initial notification.  Section 7 should be completed when the case has completed treatment.  Section 8 to be completed by the MOHW within 6 weeks of completion of treatment. Collation  Parishes, Regional Health Authority and the National Surveillance Unit will maintain databases of all notified, suspected, and confirmed Tuberculosis cases. Reporting  Parishes will submit to the regional and national levels, case investigation updates as additional data become available. Analysis  An annual Tuberculosis report is to be completed by the National Surveillance Unit, in keeping with the epidemiological requirements of the country and the reporting framework of the WHO. Data Quality  Biannual TB reports to be obtained from each Regional Health Authority containing the number of notified, confirmed, and co-infected TB cases by age-group and sex.  Biannual data validation checks are to be carried out by the National Surveillance Unit in keeping with part B of the Standards and benchmarks for tuberculosis surveillance and vital registration systems (WHO).

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 99 CHAPTER: VIII LABORATORY PROCEDURE GUIDELINES 8.1 Tuberculosis Laboratory Network 8.2 Specimen Collection 8.3 Specimen Handling Storage and Transport 8.4 Smear Microscopy 8.5 PCR, Culture and, Drug Sensitivity Testing (DST)

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 100 8.1 Tuberculosis Laboratory Network There is a TB laboratory network that consists of three levels: a) Peripheral/Hospital Laboratories b) National Public Health Laboratory c) Reference Laboratory The responsibilities of the peripheral hospital laboratory are: 1. Maintain a Biosafety Level 2 2. Ziehl Neelson (ZN) staining of smears and recording results. 3. Participate in internal and external quality control 4. Notification to Parish Health Department of all positive results 5. Maintain laboratory TB register 6. Prepare reports (monthly, quarterly and annual) and submit to NPHL 7. Refer smears to NPHL for validation The peripheral hospital laboratories are:  Mandeville Regional Hospital  St. Ann’s Bay Hospital  Cornwall Regional Hospital  University Hospital of the West Indies The responsibility of the National Public Health Laboratory  Maintain a Biosafety Level 3  Prepare concentrated or direct smears for ZN microscopy and record results  The identification of Mycobacteria tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and drug susceptibility testing  Identification of mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis (MOTT)  Support training of peripheral laboratory staff in microscopy  Participate in internal and external quality control  Provide external quality control for peripheral laboratories  Provide drug susceptibility testing to monitor treatment programme  Document cure at end of treatment The responsibility of the Reference Laboratory  Maintain a Biosafety Level 3  Support training of laboratory staff at all levels  The identification of Mycobacteria tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and drug susceptibility testing through PCR or liquid or solid culture methods

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 101  Identification of mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis (MOTT) and drug susceptibility testing through liquid or solid culture methods  Provide drug susceptibility testing to monitor treatment programme  Provide external quality control  Collaborate with a WHO recognized Supranational Laboratory for external quality assessment (EQA)  Support research and molecular typing Samples a. Types of samples collected include: i. Sputum or other respiratory samples ii. CSF, spinal I para-spinal I intra-cerebral material* iii. Gastric washings iv. Lymph node or other tissue samples or tissue fluids* v. Blood or bone marrow* vi. Bone* vii. Urine viii. Faeces (fresh or frozen) * Refer to the National Public Health Laboratory for guidance on collection of sample and suitability.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 102 8.2 Specimen Collection Proper specimen collection, storage and transport are critical in order to produce laboratory results that clinicians can rely on for definitive diagnosis and treatment decisions. Sputum or other appropriate specimens should be collected from the affected site as detailed in Table 8.2.1 below. Contact the NPHL for guidance in appropriate specimen collection and transportation. Sputum Sample Collection Process The first specimen is taken before the patient leaves as he/she may not return and this may be the only opportunity to do a smear. The second specimen is collected by the patient on arising the next morning before eating. The patient should be instructed to rinse the mouth with plain water, no antiseptic mouthwashes or toothpaste. Sputum is coughed up from deep in the chest and deposited in the container. Spit, saliva or post-nasal discharges are not acceptable. Important details to note for specimen collection include:  Ensure that no one is standing in front of the patient producing the sputum.  Explain to the patient that spit or saliva is not suitable and to avoid contaminating the outside of the container with sputum (if the outside of the container is contaminated, discard and repeat procedure using a fresh container).  Patients should be requested to rinse out their mouths first with water, if they have been chewing food immediately before sputum collection.  Ask patient to cough deeply, clear the back of the throat and produce about 5- 10ml of sputum in the container. Repeat the procedure until a sufficient amount of sputum is obtained.  Patients should not use antiseptic mouthwashes immediately prior to providing a sputum specimen. Techniques used when sputum is difficult to obtain include: 1. Bronchoscopy specimens 2. Gastric washings - particularly important for children 3. Sputum induction - particularly important for children 4. Laryngeal swab (not ideal) These techniques, however, should only be conducted in hospital settings.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 103 Table 8.2.1: Specimen Collection and Transport for Laboratory Testing Specimen Type Specimen Requirements Special Instructions Unacceptable Specimens Sputum Collect 3 specimens (spot, morning, spot) consisting of 5 – 10ml each in a sterile screw cap, leak proof container. Refrigerate or transport rapidly to prevent overgrowth of normal flora. Patient should rinse mouth with water before collecting sputum to minimize the contamination. Aerosol (saline) induced specimen should be performed only in enclosed area with precautions taken to avoid exposure. The patient inhales slowly and deeply through the mouth and then coughs at will, vigorously and deeply. Sputum is collected in a sterile container. Pooled specimens. Food particles, residues and other extraneous matter. Specimen in waxed containers may produce false positive results. Unrefrigerated specimens more than 24 hours old may produce contaminated results when cultured. Tracheal or laryngeal aspirates, bronchial lavage Collect 3 specimens from patient. Submit 5 – 10 ml in sterile screw cap container. Refrigerate or transport rapidly to prevent overgrowth. These specimens are collected by trained personnel. Pooled specimens. Food particles, residues and other extraneous matter. Specimen in waxed containers may produce false positive results. Unrefrigerated specimens more than 24 hours old may produce contaminated results when cultured.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 104 Specimen Type Specimen Requirements Special Instructions Unacceptable Specimens Gastric Lavage Submit 10mls or more in a sterile screw cap container; without any preservative; neutralized if more than 4 hours before specimen will be processed. Collect 3 consecutive days soon after patient awakens and while fasting in order to obtain sputum during sleep. Use sterile saline for lavage. Neutralize the specimen 100 mg sodium carbonate, if time between collection and processing will exceed 4 hours. Specimen over 4 hours old that is not neutralized. Body fluids - spinal, pleural, pericardial, synovial, ascitic, blood, pus, marrow and aspirates Submit at least 10- 15ml in a sterile screw cap container, without any preservative. Disinfect site with alcohol if collection is made with syringe and needle. Blood collected with heparin or sodium polyanethol sulfonate may be inoculated into appropriate blood culture medium for detection of mycobacteria. Coagulated blood or blood collected in EDTA which inhibits mycobacterial growth. Tissue Submit 1g tissue without fixative or preservative. Place in a sterile container and transport immediately to the NPHL. Collect the specimen aseptically. Do not immerse the specimen in saline or wrap in gauze. Do not freeze. Specimens in formalin.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 105 Specimen Type Specimen Requirements Special Instructions Unacceptable Specimens Urine Submit a clean catch urine in sterile screw cap container. Collect either a single early morning voided midstream sample or the total first morning specimen. Multiple single specimens may be required to optimize yield. Wash external genitals before voiding to minimize contamination. Specimen should be immediately refrigerated. Specimen contaminated with faecal matter. Catheter urine. Wound Skin lesions (tissue) and aspirate No specific volume requirements. Skin should be cleaned with alcohol before aspiration of material with syringe. Pus or exudate may be used if volume of tissue is inadequate. Specimen in Amies, Stuarts transport medium. (PAHO 2010) Labelling of Specimens and Forms Ensure containers and requisition forms are labelled and completed as detailed below. Label each container with: 1. Patient's name 2. Patient’s age 3. Patient’s registration number 4. Specimen type 5. Date of collection 6. Hospital or clinic name Information to be provided on requisition forms: 1. Patient’s name

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 106 2. Patient’s age 3. Patient’s registration 4. Sample number 5. Specimen type 6. Date of collection 7. Institution address 8. Parish 9. Referring physician 10. Clinical data 11. Treatment status 12. HIV status

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 107 8.3 Specimen Handling and Transportation Specimen containers must be securely tightened, properly labeled and placed in biohazard specimen bags. The following procedures must be applied:  Wear protective gear during receipt and inspection of incoming specimens  Ensure that sample corresponds with information provided on form  Inspect the container for signs of leakage. If mass leakage is evident discard the container by autoclaving.  Disinfect the outside of the container with a suitable disinfectant (10% bleach)  Record specimen details in appropriate laboratory records All invasive specimens such as bone marrow and other tissue, must be transported to the NPHL immediately. Sputum specimens are taken to the laboratory on the same day to prevent contamination, if there is a delay it should be refrigerated at 2-80 C and sent to the laboratory within 24-48 hours. Each specimen should be accompanied with a Tuberculosis Laboratory requisition form which is fully completed. Ensure the containers are securely tightened and placed in biohazard specimen bags. Specimens should not be wrapped in forms. The outside of the specimen container may be contaminated with sputum and should be handled with caution. The outside of the contaminated container may be wiped with bleach solution. All specimens must be transported upright at 2-80C.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 108 8.4 Smear Microscopy The Ziehl-Neelsen is a simple stain that detects acid fast bacilli (AFB) and can be used to identify positive smears in all laboratories Sputum smear microscopy for tuberculous bacilli is positive when there are at least 10,000 organisms per ml of sputum. The sputum smear positivity rates in TB/HIV co-infected patients depend on the degree of immunocompromised. Slide reporting The number of bacilli seen in a smear reflects disease severity and patient infectivity. Therefore, it is important to record the number of bacilli seen on each smear. Table 8.4.1 below shows the standard method of reporting using 1,000 x magnification for Ziehl- Neelsen smears. Table 8.4.1: Standard Method of Reporting Using 1,000 x Magnification for Ziehl- Neelsen Smears Number of Bacilli Microscopy Fields Result Reported Nil AFB per 100 oil immersion fields 0 1 – 9 AFB per 100 oil immersion fields Actual or number of AFB seen 10 - 99 AFB per 100 oil immersion fields + (1+) 1-10 AFB per oil immersion field ++ (2+) ˃ 10 AFB per oil immersion field +++ (3+) Laboratory technicians should examine all three sputum samples from presumed TB case. Results as indicated in Table 8.4.1 are made available to the clinician and the MOHW Surveillance Unit within 24 hours.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 109 8.5 PCR, Culture, and Drug Sensitivity Testing (DST) Mycobacterial PCR and culture are more sensitive than smear microscopy and provide a definitive diagnosis of TB. They are therefore seen as the gold standard for bacteriological confirmation. The modality for identification and DST of MTBC is dependent on burden of disease. The GeneXpert test is a PCR test for TB, which detects the presence of TB DNA as well as testing for the resistance to Rifampin. The GeneXpert is used to diagnose individuals suspected of having MDR-TB, HIV associated TB, all paediatric and new cases (See Appendix IV). Solid or liquid culture can be utilized for second line drug susceptibility testing and provide bacteriological confirmation of drug resistant TB. Specimens for DST will be referred to a reference laboratory or supranational laboratory. The final report should be disseminated within one working day of identification being complete. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 110 CHAPTER: IX MONITORING AND ADHERENCE TO TREATMENT

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 111 CHAPTER: IX MONITORING AND ADHERENCE TO TREATMENT 9.1 DOTS Five Point Strategy 9.2 Procedure for Treatment Monitoring- In Hospital 9.3 Procedure for Treatment Monitoring- During Continuation Phase 9.4 Expected Treatment Outcome in TB Cases 9.5 Recording and Reporting 9.6 Cohort Analysis Treatment Outcome of TB Patients 9.7 Key Targets

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 112 9.1 DOTS Five Point Strategy The acronym "DOT' means Directly Observed Treatment, in which a patient is monitored to ensure that the tablets are taken. This ensures that a TB patient takes the right drugs and the right dosage at the right intervals. Jamaica uses a modified approach to DOTS in TB management. A summary of this is outlined in Figure 9.1.1 below DOTS is conducted in the initial phase of treatment in the hospital and in the continuation phase that is completed in the community. Figure 9.1.1: DOTS Five Point Strategy 1. GOJ Commitment to National Tuberculosis Programme 2. Case Detection - by sputum smear microscopy after examination of TB suspects general health 3. Standardised short-course chemotherapy - to all smear positive TB cases under proper case management conditions 4. Regular uninterrupted supply - of all essential anti-TB drugs 5. Recording and reporting system - enabling assessment of all patients and monitoring and evaluation of programme performance

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 113 Directly observed treatment is necessary in all phases of TB treatment:  Initial Phase - During the two-month intensive phase of all new smear positive cases, four drugs (Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol - RIPE) are administered.  Continuation Phase - During the four-months continuation phase for all new smear positive cases two drugs (Rifampin and Isoniazid) are used.  Re-treatment - Throughout the entire re-treatment regimen, RIPE are administered for two months, 2 drugs (Rifampin and Isoniazid) for four months. DOTS should be adapted to patient needs and working conditions of health care workers to avoid treatment interruptions.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 114 9.2 Procedure for Treatment Monitoring - In Hospital 1. Patients should be educated about DOTS. 2. Confidentiality must be ensured so that direct observation of treatment is acceptable to the patient. 3. After producing a negative smear, patients should be discharged from the hospital with a prescription for two month’s supply of anti-TB medication. The medication should be free of charge. At the time of discharge, patients get a two month's appointment date to return for medical assessment. 4. Prior to discharge, a meeting should be held between patient, relatives, preferably primary and secondary health care workers, to discuss the continuation phase. Issues to be discussed include:  Need for a supervisor  Responsibility of the patient  Frequency of follow-up  Potential problems the patients may face during treatment  Designated health care liaison

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 115 9.3 Procedure for Treatment Monitoring - During the Continuation Phase 1. The hospital should prepare a discharge summary in triplicate and copies sent to the following:  Patient docket  Patient  Relevant parish health department A treatment card is provided to the patient. Home visits by the public health nurse and hospital visits by the patient are documented on the card. 2. The discharged patient should report to the nearest health centre to his home with the discharge summary. 3. The person in charge of the health centre should register the patient for management and send a Class 1 notification to the health department. 4. A DOTS observer is to be assigned to the case (if not yet done) to monitor the continuation phase. A meeting is to be held with the patient and relatives to decide on the assignment of the DOTS observer. 5. Each patient should be observed taking medication daily or a minimum of three times weekly. 6. The DOTS Observer must complete a daily DOT log. The log consists of the patient’s name and address, medication and schedule (observed, not observed, not available), time, side effects, other comments and the health care worker’s initials. 7. The DOTS Observer must count the remaining tablets to confirm that the reported number of tablets taken is correct. 8. Patients should be reminded about medical outpatient appointments and assisted to make transportation arrangements (if indicated). 9. Patients and family should be educated about taking the medication as prescribed. 10. The DOTS Observer should explain and arrange for the patient to provide sputum samples at designated intervals to monitor treatment responses. Arrangements can include provision of sputum specimen containers, explanation of collection process, storage and transportation to the laboratory. This is outlined in Table 9.3.1 below,

Enquiries should be made about any incidence of adverse drug reaction. Any adverse reactions should be reported through the MOHW pharmacovigilance form available at the MOHW website (See Appendix V) and submitted to the MOHW. 12. Patients reporting adverse drug reactions should be referred to the doctor. 13. Treatment defaulters should be located and encouraged to return. 14. The DOTS observer must report to the public health nurse in charge of the case concerning the patient's adherence to treatment, on a minimum monthly basis. 15. The DOTS observers must complete and submit the TB treatment card to the public health nurse. 16. The DOTS observer must report any abnormal findings to the public health Nurse within 24 hours.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 117 9.4 Expected Treatment Outcome in TB Cases The treatment outcomes for TB are detailed in Table 9.4.1 Table 9.4.1: Expected Treatment Outcomes in TB cases Treatment Outcome Description Cured A pulmonary TB patient with bacteriologically confirmed TB at the beginning of treatment who was smear- or culture-negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion. Treatment Completed A TB patient who completed treatment without evidence of failure BUT with no record to show that sputum smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion were negative, either because tests were not done or because results are unavailable. Treatment Failed A TB patient whose sputum smear or culture is positive at month 5 or later during treatment Died A TB patient who dies for any reason before starting or during the course of treatment. Loss to Follow-up A TB patient who did not start treatment or whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more. Not Evaluated A TB patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned. This includes cases “transferred out” to another treatment unit as well as cases for whom the treatment outcome is unknown to the reporting unit. Treatment Success The sum of patients who are cured and those who have completed treatment

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 118 9.5 Recording and Reporting Accurate record keeping on all patients, maintenance of registers and reporting as per schedule are minimum requirements. Reports are used for monitoring, evaluation, planning and budgeting purposes. Reports are generated from the tuberculosis registers and field records. At each level of the treatment monitoring process, a treatment register should be established to collect data for cohort analysis. It is important that all registers are kept updated with complete, accurate and reliable data. List of Monitoring Records The areas listed must maintain a Tuberculosis Register:  Laboratory Register  Health Centre  Hospital  District/Zone  Parish  Regional  National The following forms and reports are required:  TB Sputum Culture Request Form  Class 1 Notification Form  TB Case Investigation Form  Contact tracing log book  Quarterly case notification reports  Quarterly report on treatment - cohort analysis Each parish should maintain a TB register (Appendix VI). The register should have a section for treatment outcomes. On submission of the reports from the health centre and district/zones, the reports should be compiled by the Parish TB Coordinator on a monthly, quarterly and annual basis and submitted to the Medical Officer of Health. The district quarterly case-finding report and treatment outcomes are submitted through the parish MOs(H) to the regional epidemiologist/surveillance officer, National Surveillance Unit and the National TB Programme. Presently the TB Parish registers are used to monitor patient’s adherence to treatment schedule.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 119 With the aim of developing a feasible local system, there are plans to carry out the following:  Monitoring of patient usage and the development of a formalized DOTS Programme to take appropriate action.  Exploring linkages with the use of adherence counsellors (HIV/ AIDS Programme).

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 120 9.6 Cohort Analysis/Treatment Outcome of TB Patients Cohort analysis on treatment outcomes should be done every quarter and at the end of the year. A Cohort of TB patients consists of all the sputum smear positive or smear negative and Xpert positive (as in HIV/TB coinfection) pulmonary cases registered during a quarter. New and previously treated patients form separate cohorts. An evaluation at the end of treatment (6 or 8 months) outcome takes place about three (3) months after all patients in the cohort have completed their course of treatment.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 121 9.7 Key Targets Targets of the WHO END TB strategy to end the global TB Epidemic include: 1. Reduction in the number of TB deaths by 95% by 2035 compared with 2015. 2. Reduction in TB incidence rate by 90% by 2035 compared with 2015. 3. By 2035 to have 0% of TB affected families facing catastrophic costs due to TB. WHO Global Priority Indicators to Monitor END TB Strategy Ending the TB epidemic is included in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030 under Goal 3. To monitor the implementation of the END TB strategy, WHO recommended the use of the global priority indicators and targets (WHO 2015) outlined in Table 9.7.1, of which all countries should aim to reach by 2025. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 124 10.1 The Drug Logistic Cycle The essential task of NTP managers is always to ensure a complete curative course of chemotherapy for all detected and registered TB patients. To accomplish the task of ensuring regular supply of anti TB drugs and their appropriate use, each step of the drug logistic cycle (WHO, 1998) shown in Figure 10.1.1 below must be followed (Trebucq & Rambert 2001). Figure 10.1.1: The Drug Logistic Cycle

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 125 10.2 Choice Choice is dependent on:  Information coming out of laboratories - TB strains and what are the drug resistant strains if any.  Efficacy of available drugs Estimated Quantity of Drugs and Laboratory Supplies The quantity of drugs, reagents and supplies is estimated based on:  The target population which is estimated using the TB register and the Hospital Active Surveillance (HAS)  National treatment protocol algorithm  Trend analyses Monitoring Monitoring (responsibility of the clinicians and the laboratory) with feedback to the relevant stakeholders (MOHW Standards and Regulations Division) of drug effectiveness is necessary to ensure appropriate preventative and corrective action (See Appendix VIII – Pharmacovigilance Form).

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 126 10.3 Purchasing The National Health Fund (NHF) is responsible for the purchasing of drugs. Laboratory supplies are procured through the NPHL local laboratory budget. Purchasing of drugs and laboratory supplies will be according to GOJ guidelines and timelines with respect to the tender process using the restricted tender method. The quality of drugs must be maintained and must meet the standards set by the Standards and Regulations Division of the MOHW. Budgetary allocations must be ensured under GOJ financial arrangements (budgetary and extra budgetary). Close collaboration between NTP manager and procurement officers is important. It must be ensured that the national drug formulary contains the essential drugs (both first and second line drugs) and is regularly updated. Currently not all second line drugs are included in the national drug formulary. A separate tender for anti-tuberculosis drugs is performed, because:  The demand comes from a programme that has precise conditions.  To ensure that drugs are supplied in the required quantity and time frame, thus allowing patients to follow their treatment as recommended.  There are very few manufacturers of quality drugs, and a restricted tender is suitable.  The drugs are given free of charge and receive specific funding, and a separate tender facilitates their management.  The tender is the final point of a process that involves several different public departments, all of whom have a say in the final result. Monitoring The tender process must be closely monitored and post marketing surveillance must be carried out.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 127 10.4 Management of Stocks Consistent monitoring of stock is essential. A reorder level based on usage rate, lead time, minimum and maximum stock levels, buffer/ safety stock must be implemented. Constant liaison between purchaser and NTP as well as with relevant ministries is necessary to maintain adequate stock levels. The management of anti-tuberculosis drugs is based on theoretical consumption, i.e., it is linked to the number of tuberculosis patients on treatment during a defined time period. The quantity of anti-tuberculosis drugs that needs to be ordered depends on several factors:  The number of tuberculosis patients detected and notified in the HAS  The projected number of patients to be diagnosed for the period being quantified  The standardised treatment regimens used and set out in the NTP manual, and the fixed-dose combinations used  The quantity of drugs currently stocked at the central level  The reserve stock required  The drug consumption from the moment the order is made to the moment it arrives (this depends on the transport time)  The frequency of the ordering  The budget

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 128 10.5 Distribution and Storage The following factors are very important:  Appropriate storage conditions should be maintained - temperature and humidity  Control of expiry date  Reserve stock  Implementation of first expired first out (FEFO) principle  Control of handling and transport at all levels  Implementation of drug accounting system at all levels (where drugs are stored or administered) Where feasible, pre-packaging in patient specific dosages is advised to avoid wastage. Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 131 11.1 Parish/Local Level The implementation of NTP policies and guidelines occur at the service level. All Health Care Workers  Suspect and detect Tuberculosis among patients reporting for health care and take all necessary and appropriate measures for the examination of those patients.  Educate and examine household contacts of patients diagnosed with Tuberculosis.  Manage patients upon instructions from the clinician/medical officer and the Tuberculosis coordinator.  Encourage and supervise and/or arrange the supervision of patients for directly observed therapy.  Educate Tuberculosis patients on the need for regular attendance and on the importance of adherence to treatment.  Ensure that treatment progress is monitored periodically, according to the NTP guidelines.  Identify patients who need to be referred to a medical officer with regards to complications of Tuberculosis, according to the guidelines of the NTP.  Maintain the Tuberculosis register at the various levels of the health service (health centre, hospital, laboratory, district, parish and regional).  Locate and return to treatment those patients who are irregular in attendance.  Ensure that records of the attendance, treatment and sputum results are kept in the appropriate registers and files.  Conduct health education to new patients and their household contacts on the importance of early diagnosis and the possibilities of cure.  Participate in public education on Tuberculosis and its management.  Any other duties pertaining to the implementation of the national TB programme guidelines Hospital Staff  Notify suspected cases as Class 1 Notifiable Disease, on suspicion, to the relevant Health Department and National Surveillance Unit.  Educate patients, caregivers and family about TB, DOTS, treatment regimens and the possibility of cure with adequate treatment.  Arrange meeting with patient, relatives, primary and secondary care health workers concerning the continuation phase of treatment in the community.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 132  Ensure completion of the discharge summary in triplicate (one copy to be sent to the relevant Health Department, one copy to be given to the patient and one copy to be retained in the patient docket).  Ensure that patient gets medications free-of-charge and is given an appointment date for clinical review.  Any other duties pertaining to the implementation of the National TB Programme guidelines. Health Centre/Health District Supervisory Public Health Nurse  Receive notification of cases in respective areas and enter information in the Parish TB Register.  Assign an appropriate DOTS Observer to each case taking into account decisions taken at the meeting with relatives and clinicians.  Supervise DOTS Observer's functions through review of Treatment Cards, field visits, etc.  Provide monthly reports to the Parish TB Coordinator (on notifications, investigations, monitoring of cases, DOTS, etc.).  Ensure case investigation and contact investigation are performed, and submit relevant reports within time lines set out in NTP Guidelines.  Ensure adequate supplies of personal protective equipment (PPE) for suspected case/contact investigation.  Any other duties pertaining to the implementation of the national TB programme guidelines. DOTS Observer  Educate patients about TB, DOTS and the importance of compliance to treatment guidelines  Monitor the taking of medication by cases through direct observation.  Ensure accurate completion of the individual TB Treatment Card.  Supervise adherence to medication through tablet counts and other methods.  Make note of and report any incidences of adverse drug effects to the PHN.  Report weekly to PHN on the adherence of the cases to the continuation phase regimen.  Ensure that patient keeps medical appointments and fulfils laboratory and other requests.  Submit completed treatment card to health centre or public health nurse at completion of continuation phase of treatment.  Locate and persuade defaulters to return to treatment.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 133  Any other duties pertaining to the implementation of the national TB programme guidelines. Medical Officer (Health) At the parish level, the Medical Officer (Health) is responsible for planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the TB programme.  Ensure the development of an annual work plan for TB programme management (including procurement, financing/budgeting, and establishment of targets in keeping with national performance targets).

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 134  Ensure that TB programme is implemented at parish level in keeping with NTP policies and guidelines.  Monitor TB programme planning, implementation and evaluation activities of the parish TB coordinator.  Check and endorse all Class 1 Disease Notifications including TB notifications.  Conduct field visits at hospitals to ensure Hospital Active Surveillance is conducted.  Review all case investigation reports for quality, completeness and timeliness.  Collect and analyze all monthly, quarterly and annual reports submitted by parish TB coordinator, prior to submission to Regional or National Level.  Monitor the TB programme for achievement of targets and indicators.  Collaboratively formulate strategies to address issues impacting the implementation of the TB programme in the parish.  Reconcile parish register along with TB coordinator quarterly.  In collaboration with parish coordinator, conduct quarterly review of the TB programme.  Submit quarterly reports to the Regional Technical Director (RTD), Regional Epidemiologist and National TB Coordinator simultaneously.  Ensure adequate supplies/drugs for TB case management in the parish.  Any other duties pertaining to the implementation of the national TB programme guidelines.

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 141 Monitoring and Evaluation of TB Control Programme Monitoring is the routine tracking of the information about the TB Programme. Evaluation is the assessment of the efficiency and effectiveness of the interventions under the Programme. Monitoring and Evaluation should be done at all levels:  Parish  Regional  National 12.1 Monitoring and Evaluation at the Parish Level The Parish Coordinator is responsible for monitoring and evaluation at the parish level. The Parish Coordinator needs to ensure that the following activities are undertaken:  TB notifications meet programme requirements for case investigation  Records are maintained  Field Investigations are completed and reports submitted  Reports are compiled and submitted to regional health authority and the national surveillance unit on a timely basis  Availability of drugs and supplies e.g. PPD, anti-TB medication and lab supplies (in stock).  Budget prepared  DOTS requirements being met - staffing, traveling etc.  Audits of hospitals - HAS procedure and field visits  Case investigations reviewed for quality, completeness and timeliness.  Submission of monthly, quarterly and annual reports e.g. cohort analysis, monthly case findings etc.  Monitor the implementation of set work plan for achievement of targets and indicators.  Strategies formulated to combat barriers to success  Monthly reconciliation of parish register with NTB coordinator  Develop a LTBI register for the parish  Quarterly review of the TB surveillance programme  Conduct quarterly review of treatment outcomes

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 142 12.2 Monitoring and Evaluation at the Regional Level The Regional Technical Director (RTD) plays an important role in monitoring and evaluation of the TB Programme at the Regional Health Authority. The RTD or their designate should ensure that the following activities are undertaken:  Monitoring of the frequency of submission of reports from the parishes  Analysis of parish reports for achievements of indicators and targets set out in work plan  Audit of parish TB surveillance system  Preparation of budget

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 143 12.3 Monitoring and Evaluation at the National Level The objectives of monitoring and evaluation include:  To determine the implementation of policy decisions  To determine the status of implementation of surveillance strategies  To determine the achievement of targets and indicators set out in the work plan  To conduct an audit of the TB Programme on a biennial basis A multi-stakeholder TB Diagnostic Committee should be established with a secretariat and additional key stakeholders. The committee will meet biannually. The secretariat will include:  Director TCS HSTU MOHW  National TB Programme Coordinator – (Programme Development Officer HSTU)  MO(H) representative from WRHA  MO(H) representative from SERHA  Senior Medical Officer of National Chest Hospital In addition to the secretariat the TB Diagnostic Committee will include the following:  Kingston Public Hospital Infectious Disease Specialist  UWI Pulmonologist  Laboratory  Representative from HIV Programme  Nursing representative  National surveillance unit representative This TB Diagnostic committee will review the following:  Hospital treatment  Community treatment  Defaulters  Laboratory and radiological results  Classification of cases  Treatment outcomes The functions of the TB diagnostic committee are supported by the National TB Coordinator. Activities to be undertaken include:  Preparation of quarterly, annual and special reports as well as process evaluation  Provide feedback from evaluations  Checks on data quality

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 144  Analysis of trends in TB  Utilization of available and appropriate technology for data storage and retrieval  Research  Preparation of programme budget

Guidelines for the Management of Tuberculosis in the Jamaican Population 157 Definitions for Tuberculosis Treatment History New case: A patient who has never been treated for TB or who has taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. Previously treated patients: Patients who have received 1 month or more of anti-Tb drugs in the past. i. Relapse patients: A patient previously treated for TB who was declared cured or treatment completed at the end of their most recent course of treatment, and are now diagnosed with a recurrent episode of TB. ii. Treatment after failure patients: A patient who has been previously treated for Tb and whose treatment failed at the end of their most recent course of treatment. iii. Treatment after loss to follow up patients: A patient who has been previously treated for TB and were declared loss to follow-up at the end of their most recent course of treatment (previously known as treatment after default patients). iv. Other previously treated patients: Patients who have been previously treated for TB but whose outcome after their most recent course of treatment is unknown or undocumented Definitions of treatment outcomes for drug-susceptible TB i. Cured: A pulmonary TB patient with bacteriologically confirmed TB at the beginning of treatment who has was smear or culture negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion. ii. Treatment completed: A TB patient who completed treatment without evidence of failure, but with no record to show that sputum smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion were negative, either because tests were not done or because results are unavailable. iii. Died: A TB patient who dies for any reason before starting or during the course of treatment. iv. Treatment failed: A TB patient whose sputum or culture is positive at month 5 or later during treatment. v. Loss to follow-up: A TB patient who did not start treatment or whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more. vi. Not evaluated: A TB patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned. This includes cases “transferred out” to another treatment unit as well as cases for whom the treatment outcome is unknown to the reporting unit. vii. Treatment success: A TB patient who is cured or who has completed treatment.

Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 7 FOREWORD The Elimination of Mother to Child Transmission (EMTCT) of HIV & Syphilis by 2015 in the Americas continues to be the aim of the Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV & Syphilis (PMTCT) programme in Jamaica. This WHO target has been subsumed into Jamaica’s National Integrated Strategic Plan (NISP) for HIV & Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH), ensuring the efforts of the HIV/STI/TB UNIT (HSTU) are in tandem with those of the Family Health Unit (FHU) and the National Family Board (NFBP); the two main providers of SRH care in the island. At the national level, confirmation of positive cases of HIV & Syphilis in infants continues with a robust notification process through the National Surveillance Unit (NSU). This serves a dual purpose as it also enables the validation of field reports received directly by the HSTU. At the sub-national level, the PMTCT programme begins with provider initiated testing & counselling (PITC) during the antenatal period at both public and private health care facilities. Documentation of positivity rates for both HIV & Syphilis, appropriate treatment inclusive of drugs and dosing, outcome and final status of delivered infants are all recorded in the monthly PMTCT report submitted to the HSTU via an email reporting account and a recently introduced electronic reporting account. Challenges specific to Syphilis such as comparatively lower testing rates than HIV and poor documentation of the clinical follow-up and treatment of the mother/infant pair have been countered with the introduction of Maternal Syphilis and Syphilis Exposed Infant Registers in the last quarter of 2017. PMTCT Coordinators, Nurses, Clinicians and relevant support staff such as, Regional HIV Coordinators, Contact Investigators, Social Workers and Adherence Counsellors have been trained in the use of these new and updated data collection tools. The relevant private sector health care workers were also included, with the HSTU being cognizant of their inclusion for an all-encompassing national response. The EMTCT Oversight Committee inclusive of paediatricians, gynaecologists, past JaPPAIDS committee members, donors and NGO representatives continue to give technical expertise and guidance to the nation’s response to the epidemic. Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 9 I. INTRODUCTION

Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 10 I. INTRODUCTION Ensuring universal access to prevention, treatment, care and support services is a priority of the National HIV/STI/TB Programme in Jamaica. This involves promoting the quality delivery of Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission services island-wide, which is the main purpose of this guiding protocol for health care workers. Jamaica endorsed the initiative to eliminate vertical transmission of HIV and syphilis in all countries and territories in the Caribbean by the year 2015. The following criteria are proposed to declare elimination status for a country or territory:  Rate of MTCT for HIV equal to or below 2% OR 0.3 cases per 1000 live births for three years;  Incidence rates of congenital syphilis (including stillbirths) equal to or below 0.5 cases per 1000 live births for three years. The PMTCT of HIV programme in Jamaica commenced during July 2000 as a pilot programme/ feasibility study conducted in selected sites in four (4) parishes. In April 2003, it was expanded into a comprehensive programme that was introduced into the public health care system across the island. Approximately 1.5% to 2% of Antenatal Clinic attendees in Jamaica are estimated to be HIV positive. Without PMTCT interventions, transmission may occur: - During pregnancy (in utero): 20%-25% through maternal-foetal blood exchange - During labour and delivery (intrapartum): 60%-70% through contact of the infant’s skin and mucous membranes with infected blood or the other maternal secretions - After delivery (postpartum): 10%-15% through breastfeeding. Since 2002, with appropriate interventions, vertical transmission of HIV has been reduced nationally from 25% to less than 2%. In Jamaica, these interventions have included access to antenatal care, HIV counselling and testing in pregnancy, chemoprophylaxis with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to HIV positive pregnant women and

Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 11 also to their non-breastfed infants until four to six weeks of age. Early infant diagnosis utilizing the dried blood spot (DBS) testing which was implemented across the island commencing in late 2009, has further facilitated diagnosis of the exposed infants’ HIV status by six months of age to ensure early effect of the appropriate interventions. In addition, comprehensive health care including public access to HAART for the HIV infected woman, her children and family has significantly reduced HIV-attributable morbidity and mortality, island-wide. Recognizing that HIV/AIDS affects the whole family, the ultimate goal in HIV/AIDS Treatment and Care is the adaptation of a family-centred model of care. Therefore, emphasis should be on the multidisciplinary approach to the management of HIV infected pregnant women, their partners and their children. In addition, the PMTCT programme needs to be seamlessly linked with HIV/AIDS, reproductive health and family health services. Syphilis has long been managed within the primary health care system in Jamaica. Based on available data regarding confirmed cases of congenital syphilis, the island likely has already achieved elimination status of this condition. However, verification of this may prove difficult due to the lack of completed investigation forms for all notified cases. As a way forward with this elimination initiative, to ensure that the goals are achieved, the following are imperative:  Improved documentation for all cases, from the point of notification to the completion of investigation;  Strengthening of collaboration with the private sector;  Improved follow-up of all affected mother-infant pairs;  Implementation of rapid testing (HIV and Syphilis) at all major birthing facilities to improve access to those with suboptimal antenatal care and  Ongoing training of staff in PMTCT of HIV and syphilis. Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 14 I. PREVENTION OF VERTICAL TRANSMISSION OF SYPHILIS Congenital Syphilis is a preventable cause of stillbirths and perinatal morbidity. Syphilis passes from an infected mother to the foetus via trans placental transmission of Treponema Pallidum at any time during pregnancy and at birth. Infection can be transmitted to the foetus at any stage of the disease with the highest rates of transmission occurring during primary and secondary Syphilis. Left untreated, it is estimated that 66% of pregnant women would have adverse outcomes compared to 14% of women without Syphilis. As in the case of HIV, prevention of transmission from mother-to-child of other sexually transmitted infections is critical. In its early stages, Syphilis is asymptomatic; so a high index of suspicion, early screening and treatment are necessary to minimize complications in mother and child. Manifestations of Syphilis in pregnancy depend on the stage of disease in the mother, as well as the stage of pregnancy when the disease was acquired (See Maternal Syphilis Algorithm for the management of syphilis in pregnancy). Guidelines for the Prevention of Vertical Transmission of HIV & Syphilis, Jamaica 16 SYPHILIS TESTING IN PREGNANCY Syphilis testing is well entrenched in antenatal services offered in the primary healthcare system. Risky sexual behaviours are characterized by one or a combination of the following: o unprotected sex o multiple sex partners o engaging in commercial/transactional sex o drug/alcohol use while engaging in sexual activity  Provision of Syphilis rapid testing on labour wards for all mothers with undocumented Syphilis status  Ensuring notification and follow-up of mother-baby pairs to the closure of the case All sexual contacts reported by the Syphilis infected pregnant woman should be traced and treated accordingly. Latent and tertiary Syphilis are treated with BPG 2.4 million units IM stat for three (3) doses at one (1) week apart. The first dose has to be initiated thirty (30) days or more before delivery. Adequate treatment for PMTCT is BPG 2.4 million units IM in a single dose, initiated thirty (30) days or more before delivery.

Follow up post treatment, is also essential in assessing the adequacy of treatment and monitoring for re-infection. Maternal Syphilis is a Class 3 Notifiable Disease. Pregnant women who have known allergies to penicillin are to be referred to hospital for desensitization. All desensitization is to be done in a hospital setting only.
